#2652. Bad weather can’t be the main cause of Falcons’ ugly defeat

After the Falcons' ugly loss in Tampa Bay, plenty of discussion focused on how the weather affected their performance. A nasty rainstorm affects every team's play. Look no further than Baker Mayfield, who didn't complete a pass on three attempts and fumbled multiple times.

Instead of forcing a balanced attack, Tampa Bay solely relied on the ground game and brutalized their opponent. They adapted to the conditions and used their strengths to break a divisional rival down in the trenches. The Falcons couldn't move the ball efficiently on the ground or stop the run. That put the game in Michael Penix Jr.'s hands, and he proceeded to have the worst game of his career.

Todd Bowles' squad embraced the chaotic environment and flourished in it. Kevin Stefanski's team was rattled in it and drowned in gruesome fashion. Much more went into that abysmal performance than a rainstorm preventing them from executing.

A one-sided defeat stems from self-inflicted errors, personnel breakdowns, coaching miscues, and players not being good enough. That's what the Falcons have to accept when assessing what went wrong.

From not being able to push the ball downfield to having to adjust your footwork, a massive rainstorm will challenge how a signal caller operates in the pocket.

What it shouldn't change is how the quarterback reads the field and processes defensive looks, especially when he receives solid pass protection. Penix Jr. was completely discombobulated in the pocket, making numerous costly errors and misses.

His inability to see Alex Anzalone on his first two interceptions was perplexing. The first turnover came from Anzalone dropping off the line of scrimmage into the short area of the field. The linebacker never tried blitzing into the C-gap.

He went straight back into coverage and somehow capitalized on an errant Penix Jr. pass that was lofted into his hands. Penix Jr. didn't see him there or on the next drive, where he tried to connect with Jahan Dotson down the seam. That throw went directly to Anzalone once again for another interception.

The fourth-down interception to Jacob Parrish was the one excusable turnover, as it was a desperate heave in a collapsed pocket on a make-or-break play. There was no poor processing or decision-making. But that came back to haunt him on the final interception, where Zyon McCollum didn't bite on the fake smoke screen.

While the play design deserves criticism (more on that below), Penix Jr. used a pump fake before attempting to throw with anticipation, assuming McCollum would bite. The cornerback didn't budge and capitalized on another appalling mistake from Penix Jr.

Three of the four interceptions were squarely on the enigmatic quarterback. He had some ugly incompletions because he still doesn't consistently throw the ball well in the intermediate middle area of the field. Bad weather will limit, not ruin, a quarterback's ability to perform. Franchise quarterbacks have to prove they can overcome adversity and operate functionally in difficult circumstances. Penix Jr. failed to do that in a big divisional game.

Mother Nature doesn't impact how your linemen compete in the trenches. On both sides of the ball, the Falcons were mauled during long stretches. The undersized defensive front was bound to have issues against one of the league's more physically imposing groups. Tampa Bay's offensive line did its share of damage, but an overall team effort helped spring Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell into the open field.

Chris Godwin and Payne Durham made multiple key pin and seal blocks to create space at the second level. As Tristian Wirfs and Cody Mauch imposed their will, the skill position players blocked like demons to disorient the Falcons' attack front. Defensive linemen were getting erased in the run game.

The starting rookie linebacker tandem struggled, particularly Harold Perkins Jr., who couldn't get off his blocks and missed a few tackles. It was a humbling day for a unit missing size up front, as they didn't receive much support on the back end, with defensive backs missing tackles all over the place.

The offensive line was equally as humbled on the ground. My colleague Tre'Shon Diaz noted in his piece that Bijan Robinson averaged 2.6 yards per carry on 18 attempts if you remove his 30-yard gain. Most of his yards came from an extraordinary effort to keep his balance through a pile to produce an explosive play.

Matthew Bergeron has played better in spurts, but he has failed to live up to the lofty contract extension he received this past summer. Ryan Neuzil's physical limitations have become problematic against bigger fronts. Jake Matthews offers little as a run blocker at this point, while Jawan Taylor was repeatedly behind on his assignments. As much as the Falcons want to be fast and athletic in the trenches, the lack of sheer size and gap-moving power is glaring in these one-sided defeats.

Per The Athletic's Josh Kendall, the Falcons faced ten third- and fourth-down plays of two yards or less. They gained a grand total of four yards on those plays. That includes not converting any of their 12 third downs. It was an appalling performance that requires some serious soul-searching.

They can't be solely reliant on Penix Jr. and Charlie Woerner to sneak to convert every time. They also need to understand the challenges facing Tampa Bay's front.

No matter how much you pride yourself on running the ball, you need in-game adjustments for your game plan against specific units. Tampa Bay has one of the league's strongest run defenses. Calling runs that kept going directly toward Vita Vea was baffling.

When the Falcons produced solid gains on the ground, it came from gap-scheme runs with offensive linemen pulling and other personnel making down blocks. They also had flashes of positive gains on stretch runs. It was nowhere near what Irving and Gainwell did, but it proved to be effective in spurts.

You can't call those runs often in short-yardage situations, but more variation is needed to attack a defense playing at a top-ten level. It nearly worked in the first quarter on a third-and-two when Kyle Pitts was open downfield on a deep crosser off play action. After coolly evading a blitzing Anzalone in the pocket, Penix Jr. had the space to hit Pitts for a likely touchdown.

He sailed it well over his head with no Tampa Bay defender in sight. Although the execution wasn't there, that type of clever, aggressive play calling could make the difference in solving these frustrating woes.

What was supposed to be one of the offense's schematic strengths is a genuine liability. Stefanski and Rees were praised for how well they utilized screens in Cleveland. The timing was on point. The execution was crisp. Offensive linemen and skill-position players handled their blocking assignments while defenders chased them downfield.

Outside of Bijan Robinson's opening-day touchdown against Pittsburgh, it's hard to recall many significant screens. Opposing defenders are diagnosing them as soon as the ball is snapped. They beat opposing blocks by accelerating to the intended target before the ball arrives.

Tykee Smith blew up a screen designed for Pitts on 3rd-and-2. While Chris Blair missed his assignment, it's extremely hard to fulfill it when defensive backs like Smith instantly know where the ball is going.

Even though Penix Jr. is at fault for his final interception, the fake smoke screen was oddly designed. It's bizarre that Woerner is the primary target downfield running a wheel route. Although the design could deceive the defense, the ball is thrown in such a tight area downfield that you don't want a blocking tight end there unless he is clearly wide open on a leak play.

The coaching staff desperately needs to figure out what is wrong with the screens because the design and execution must be better for a team with limited receiving options.

#2648. Open Thread: Tracy McGrady says Kevin Garnett was more impactful than Tim Duncan

On their podcast, Cousins, 2000 NBA Slam Dunk Champion Vince Carter and and 2001 NBA Most Improved Player Tracy McGrady discuss a variety of NBA topics. The cousins (it's not just a clever name for a podcast though it is not a show hosted by Boogie Cousins, as I mistakenly originally believed) discovered their familial bond at a reunion. They played together with the Toronto Raptors a year later. Both had significant NBA careers. Tracy McGrady finished his career with the San Antonio Spurs as part of the 2013 title run.

He recently posited that though Tim Ducan is considered the greatest power forward of all time, he thinks it is a benefit of how Duncan was able to design the Spurs around him. The idea is put forth that Kevin Garnett did more than Duncan, but the titles make Duncan look the better player.

My initial reaction was to defend Duncan and dismiss McGrady as having an axe to grind or something. But after listening, I have to give him some respect. McGrady clearly states that he "look(s) at the game totally different." I cannot begin to imagine the wealth of basketball knowledge, a conversation most assuredly to float above my head and waft ad the words left his mouth.

The repost from David West puts it into perspective.

It was Tim's system. One thing I realized my year with them was that Tim built the damn thing. It was his brainchild. It was his basketball genius that made that shit the monster it was. IYKYK 🤷🏽‍♂️

It opens up the conversation. Could Tim Duncan have become the Tim Duncan of the Spurs if he had been drafted by the Boston Celtics? What about if he had left San Antonio to play in Orlando? If the environment changes, doesn't the payer change in some form or fashion?

If Kevin Garnett had been given the keys to the kingdom of Minnesota? Or been drafted first overall by Golden State (hindsight being 20/20 and all), could he have cultivated an organization than won five championships?

As a Spurs fan, I am fortunate those are just questions. Tim Duncan was drafted by the Spurs, decided to stay after considering Orlando (if Doc Rivers could go back he'd give Duncan his own private jet…hindsight being 20/20 and all), and completed a nineteen year career in San Antonio bringing more than five championships to the city. He brought a culture, and a style, and a temperament that embodies the franchise's personality.

And now we Victor Wembanyama. The most talented player of his generation, a genuine gentleman, a scholar, and a player who carries some of the great qualities that have already been associated with the Silver & Black.

Honestly, McGrady's take doesn't bother me at all. I'll take what we've got.

#2647. Our Offense vs. Their Defense: Cleveland Browns

The New Orleans Saints are returning to action after a bye week with more questions than they had to start the season. Now, this matchup with the Browns serves as a litmus test for the changes that were made during the bye, not just for the coaching staff but for the entire organization.

This game against the Browns is a really intriguing matchup for the offense because this defense is exactly what the Saints need to face right now. The Browns' biggest weakness on defense is rushing yards allowed. Cleveland ranks 24th in rushing defense in the NFL, surrendering 126.9 yards per game and 4.68 yards per carry. Just last week against the Steelers, the Browns allowed 200 rushing yards.

Everyone knows the Saints have had issues running the ball, and now, with C.J. Donaldson suffering an injury, that only compounds their rushing problems. But there may be some hope after all.

The Saints have added Audric Estime back to the roster, claiming him off waivers. Estime showed a lot of promise at the end of last season, when the Saints were struggling to run the ball, and throughout the preseason. It caught a lot of people off guard when the Saints opted to release him before the season started, but he's back now and will be a welcome addition come Sunday afternoon for an offense that is averaging only 86 rushing yards per game and ranks 28th in the NFL.

Running the ball will be very important in this game because if the Saints become one-dimensional, it will play right into the hands of the Browns. Cleveland currently has the sixth-best defense against the pass, allowing only 196 yards per game.

The Browns have been so successful in pass coverage because they have an elite interior pass rush. Mason Graham, Maliek Collins, and Adin Huntington have combined for 11 sacks. Quarterbacks cannot step up into the pocket against this defensive front, and there is consistent pressure off the edge from Isaiah McGuire, who has 3 sacks, and Jared Verse. Verse has 0 sacks right now, but he is still an edge rusher the Saints have to be aware of.

The Saints are averaging only 229 passing yards per game, which ranks 14th in the NFL. If the Saints get into the red zone, they have to convert. Cleveland allows touchdowns on 73.9% of opponents' red-zone opportunities, while the Saints are converting only 52.2% of theirs.

While Jordyn Tyson is trying to make his way back onto the playing field, Chris Olave remains one of the best receivers in the league. Over the past few weeks, his production has dipped a bit because of the attention he receives, and this week will be no different. Kellen Moore will have to find creative ways to get him open because Olave will be matched up against Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell. The Browns' cornerbacks are very physical, and Moore will have to find ways to counter that.

To win this game, the Saints will have to run the ball against this weak run defense and keep the offense balanced. They have to commit to a decent number of rushing attempts. This will help slow down Cleveland's pass rush. The Browns have 21 sacks, with 11 coming from the interior. Run at them and slow down their pass rush!

The Saints have allowed 15 sacks so far this season, and Tyler Shough is already fighting through broken bones in his non-throwing hand.

Run the ball, protect Tyler Shough, and get creative. Design plays that get your playmakers in space and work in concert with the running game. Use motions, shifts into different formations, and heavy run-action plays. Make this defense play with its eyes and not its instincts.

Will the Saints come out of this game looking like they have improved, or will it just be more of the same? Hopefully, the changes that were made will lead to better results this week.

How do you think the Saints' offense will handle this Browns defense? Do you feel good about the changes that were made during the bye week?

#2645. CSK, SRH complete four-player trade ahead of IPL 2027; Liam Livingstone, Khaleel Ahmed switch teams

Chennai Super Kings (CSK) and Sunrisers Hyderabad (SRH) have agreed to a four-player trade ahead of the IPL 2027 season, with both franchises making significant changes to their squads.Under the deal, England all-rounder Liam Livingstone and Australian seam-bowling all-rounder Jack Edwards will move to CSK, while left-arm pacer Khaleel Ahmed and Australian fast bowler Nathan Ellis will join SRH.Livingstone has been transferred to CSK for INR 6 crore, taking a substantial pay cut from the INR 13 crore at which SRH had originally acquired him.Edwards, meanwhile, will join the Chennai-based franchise at his existing fee of INR 3 crore. SRH had signed the Australian all-rounder before his international debut, but he did not get an opportunity to feature in IPL 2026 after a foot injury ruled him out of the entire season.In exchange, SRH will secure the services of Khaleel at his existing contract value of INR 4.8 crore. The left-arm pacer is familiar with the Hyderabad franchise, having represented them between 2018 and 2021.Khaleel moved to CSK ahead of IPL 2025 and made an impact with 15 wickets in 14 matches. However, his IPL 2026 campaign was cut short after he suffered a right quadriceps injury. He managed to play only five matches during the season before being ruled out.The fourth player involved in the exchange is Nathan Ellis, who will move to SRH at his existing fee of INR 2 crore. The Australian quick, known for his variations and ability to deliver in the death overs, brings considerable T20 experience to Hyderabad's pace attack.Ellis was also unavailable throughout IPL 2026 after suffering a severe hamstring injury that forced him to miss the entire tournament.The four-player exchange gives CSK two overseas all-rounders in Livingstone and Edwards, while SRH strengthen their bowling resources with the additions of Khaleel and Ellis ahead of the 2027 campaign.

#2643. Is this the best version of Lakers star Luka Dončić we've ever seen?

SACRAMENTO – The Los Angeles Lakers aren't even 10 games into the season and superstar Luka Dončić already looks to be in midseason form.

Dončić had his third-consecutive 40-point game, and fifth of the season, as he led the Lakers to a 116-103 win against the Sacramento Kings at Golden 1 Center on Wednesday, Nov. 4. He stuffed the stat sheet with 40 points, nine rebounds, seven assists, one block and one steal.

Dončić leads the league in scoring so far with 38.5 points per game. He eclipsed Michael Jordan for most points through 8 games since the 1988-89 season with his Wednesday performance (Jordan had 303, Dončić reached 308).

Simple and plain, the man is on a heater. And so are the Lakers, now 7-2, after their third straight win.

"Probably this and the entire month of March last year," Lakers head coach JJ Redick said about Dončić and his scoring streak. "I think that back-to-back we had where he closed out Houston (and) ... then we went to Miami and got in at 4 a.m., and then he had 60, I mean, that stretch was pretty magical for him, but he's playing great right now."

Lakers guard Austin Reaves thought Dončić could have poured in a 60-point night on Wednesday, blaming a slow start in the first quarter where Dončić finished with 10 points.

"He could've had 60 if he wasn't asleep in the first quarter," Reaves told reporters. "He's scored 70 in a game. He's good. He's a good basketball player. He's been doing this since he was 19."

The way he's started the season, Dončić is reminding the league what things can be like when he's healthy.

He averaged 37.5 points per game last March, including 7 out of 16 games with 40 or more points. But Dončić then suffered a season-ending Grade 2 hamstring injury on April 2. He spent the entire offseason getting his leg back to where it used to be, even forgoing international FIBA play for his home country of Slovenia.

Dončić's health has lots to do with his blazing start to the season, but he's hesitant to say it's the best he's felt in his career, now in his 9th NBA season.

"I don't know, honestly," Dončić told USA TODAY Sports. "Too early to tell, you know. But I look back and I had a whole summer to recover. A lot of stuff that I couldn't do last maybe eight years. So maybe that's where the energy is coming from."

Redick focused on adding a new aspect to his 27-year-old superstar's game to relieve some of the ballhandling and fatigue that builds from that task alone. His adjustment are paying dividends early on.

"He's doing a great job. You know, playing off the ball," Redick said. "We're trying to set off ball screens for him. Other guys... I think some of that workload from bringing the ball up against pressure every single possession ... it's very intentional."

The Kings tried various defensive schemes to slow Dončić. Kings head coach Doug Christie added a 2-2-1 full court defense that falls back into a zone in the halfcourt.

"Players like Luka have such abilities to play so many different ways that you have to give looks that constantly keep them guessing," Christie said.

"This is one best players in the world and Luka is special," he added. "You're not gonna lock him down and stop him, but you have to have the ability to frustrate him, force him into shots that we consider good shots, which are above the break threes that are contested, middy's that are contested, and live with it. But what you don't want to do is put him on free throw line."

Dončić's much-improved defense also deserves some attention. He's averaging 0.7 blocks and 1.9 steals per game early in the 2026-27 season. He's particularly been better at closing out on shots, defending ballhandlers on the drive and challenging them inside the paint.

Dončić leads the league so far in defense inside the arc, holding opponents to 21.9 percent 2-point field goal shooting, which is lower than players like Miles Bridges, LeBron James, Donovan Clingan, Ronald Holland, Victor Wembanyama and Ausar Thompson.

It's looks like the 2026-27 season could be Dončić's revenge tour with how well he's played on both sides. Through the first month of the season, he's an early favorite for MVP.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Is this the best version of Lakers star Luka Dončić we've ever seen?

#2642. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2641. Cowboys point/counterpoint: Inconsistency looms as huge obstacle

It's one thing for a football team to be inconsistent from game to game. That can make it hard to accomplish much. Being wildly inconsistent within the same game is possibly even worse.

We just saw the Dallas Cowboys wrest a stunning defeat from the jaws of what looked until halftime was going to be a pretty decent win over their nemesis, the Arizona Cardinals. They dominated things before halftime, building a 17-3 lead. The offense wasn't exactly crisp, but a couple of takeaways and some sacks let them put points up while keeping the Cards under control.

But Arizona pulled Jacoby Brissett and put Gardiner Minshew in at QB, and suddenly they were an offensive juggernaut. Dallas still managed to add 13 points to their score, but could not stop the Cards from scoring TDs on four consecutive drives. Still, thanks to a missed extra point, the Cowboys had a chance to win it in overtime, only to see their offense continue a slump that started in the fourth quarter.

This inconsistency now hangs over their heads as they visit the Indianapolis Colts next Sunday. Our Sean Martin and Tom Ryle discuss the unfortunate realities of this year's Dallas team.

Tom – It's hard to process the abject failure we witnessed at AT&T Stadium. After bottling up the Arizona offense for the most part, the Cowboys' defense just seemed to crumble once Minshew came in. What is really mystifying is how the most damage was done by running back Tyler Allgeier. Another bevy of missed tackles and bad defensive alignments let him run free. The defense had really been the main reason Dallas built a 14-point lead at half. Then it just fell apart.

Meanwhile, their offense was also displaying its own version of inconsistency. After a good showing against the admittedly depleted Philadelphia Eagles, we once again saw multiple missed opportunities. The run game went back to sleep. A rash of sacks of Dak Prescott also played a big part. We are seeing evidence that he has to have a clean pocket to make the passing game work. Once that breaks down, things go off the rails.

Now the chance for the first winning streak has been blown, they are facing another 'must win' game. The Colts do look very beatable. The challenge is that Dallas cannot play down to the level of the competition again.

Sean – Our worst nightmare has been realized, as now it requires beating the San Francisco 49ers to get back-to-back wins, and still needing until mid-November to do so. The inconsistency really makes the fan experience hard to enjoy, we have to say at this point we've been conditioned under Brian Schottenheimer to just expect a letdown after each and every win. And here's the crushing thing that goes with that too – even Schotty's wins this season aren't impressive.

There were some things to like about how the team took a workmanlike attitude out of the Eagles win, instead of getting too high like usual, but clearly this somehow didn't help them get up off the mat once hit with adversity at home against the Cardinals. That is ridiculous.

Tom – I would choose ludicrous as my description. This is a team with veteran leadership that looks rudderless. And clearly the coaching staff is doing an enormously inept job.

Although I will not tabulate any fetal barnyard fowl, I do think there is a better than even chance they will beat the Colts. Maybe by a comfortable margin, or just eking out a win. But as I said, that is hardly a given. And if they do manage to avoid an even bigger disappointment against 2-6 Indy, that, as you said, still leaves the NFCW-leading 49ers to face.

Given how things have gone this season, the most likely scenario is that they will get a win at the Colts, then get totally embarrassed by San Francisco. That is another home game for Dallas, and they have only managed one win this season in their own house.

Trying to find things to build hope on is very hard.

Sean – This game was really a wild meltdown in three parts. Early on, it didn't feel like the Cowboys had a lot of energy, but the score held at 17-3 for a while and there was some thought that maybe this would be a win stamped by the defense, which would be a welcome sight to say the least.

Then it became just trying to hold on for dear life, to the point where even a win doesn't bode all that well for seizing any momentum. My only thought at this point was that it is the Cardinals, these games are for whatever reason never easy, and let's just get the win in the bank.

Finally, the collapse was complete, and now there really is only one way to describe this upcoming Colts game as far as I'm concerned – two bad teams going at it. The Cowboys have zero quality wins and a list of bad losses that some head coaches don't compile in multiple seasons on the job, yet Schottenheimer has five and room to add more before Thanksgiving here in year two.

Tom – I for one am so tired of wasting talented players. I don't know if it's bad coaching, a failure to have a better supporting cast so the talent at the top is nullified, or maybe some kind of culture issue. Maybe some of all three, and things we just can't figure out.

I am getting an uneasy feeling that we are watching yet another season go down the drain. No, it's not just a feeling. It's a growing sense of inevitability. At least I came into this year without great hopes, believing it was always a long shot to make the playoffs with no real chance at going far.

So I'm not disappointed as much as I'm just disgusted.

Sean – Likewise Tom, my concern is about trying to get something out of this season that protects what's hopefully the best possible future for this franchise, but that feels rocky right now.

Doing virtually no work on one side of the ball (offense) in the offseason won't be an option; by the time we slog our way through this latest wasted season, the offense is going to have concerns, question marks, and need to be shaken up. It could very well have a new head coach, offensive coordinator, or both on top of all that.

The best path forward for the defense is likely still to get to a second season with the same coordinator in place, but is it too much to ask for the coordinator earning that chance to not give up 33 points to the Cardinals?

This organization is going to have a hard time selling a year 12 for Dak Prescott being the one they finally use to get over the hump, and we don't even know if that will include both CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens remaining together. They sure didn't seem interested in using this duo to their advantage against the Cardinals anyway. Kenny Clark and Quinnen Williams will be a year older, and they've needed EDGE help since the start of this season, another thing that hurt them in this latest loss.

Normally, the generic answer here would just be that seeing which players continue to play hard through adversity is always something a team can build off of. Right now though, that just feels like a play into the whole "culture build" that Schotty sold us a bill of goods on, and appeasing to a coach long term that doesn't have a long term future here as far as any of the fan base is concerned.

*Gulps* We might have to continue having the conversation that the best thing for this current 2026 team is to still try and win the NFC East, which physically makes me feel gross to even say.

#2640. Keep an eye on these 4 QBs chasing history on Sunday

When looking at the NFL, Week 9 will jump off the page when looking at the quarterbacks who are looking to reach career milestones on Sunday. Let's look at who is chasing history this week.

Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen leads all quarterbacks in NFL history with 88 rushing touchdowns. He also ranks second-most in rushing yards with 4,991 since entering the NFL in 2018. With at least 9 more rushing yards against the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football, Allen would join a list that includes Lamar Jackson, Michael Vick, Cam Newton, and Russell Wilson as the only QBs in NFL history with at least 5,000 rushing yards.

Cincinnati Bengals QB Joe Burrow leads the NFL in passing touchdowns this season with 20 so far. That includes 13 touchdown passes over his last three games. If Burrow throws 4 more touchdown passes against the Atlanta Falcons in Madrid on Sunday, he will become the fourth quarterback in NFL history with at least 4 touchdown passes in consecutive games. Joining Peyton Manning, Tom Brady, and Dan Marino.

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes leads the NFL in touchdown passes since joining the league in 2017, with 325, including postseason games. If Mahomes throws 3 more touchdown passes against the New York Jets in Week 9, he will surpass Peyton Manning for the most touchdown passes in a player's first ten seasons.

New England Patriots QB Drake Maye ranks tied for second among quarterbacks with three rushing touchdowns this season and tied for fifth with 15 touchdown passes. Entering Week 9, he has recorded two touchdown passes and a rushing touchdown in each of his last two games. With 2 more touchdown passes and a rushing touchdown on Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, Maye would become the sixth quarterback since 1970 with two or more passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown in three consecutive games.

#2634. Who has the edge between the Patriots and Packers?

This weekend will be one of celebration for the New England Patriots. On Saturday, former tight end Rob Gronkowski will be inducted into the organization's Hall of Fame, followed by an event honoring the 10-year anniversary of the club's 2016 Super Bowl victory.

Will the 2026 version of the team be able to add to the good feelings against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday? The oddsmakers seem to believe so, and the statistical comparison also favors them in certain areas.

However, a closer head-to-head look shows that a victory is not a guarantee.

Patriots pass offense vs. Packers pass defense: This is probably the pick that has the biggest potential to come back to bite us. However, we are not entirely confident in New England's passing offense against the Packers. Granted, Drake Maye has been fantastic since the calendar turned to October and Mack Hollins might be coming back from injured reserve to bolster a shorthanded receiver group, but this is not the Dolphins they are going up against: Green Bay has been disruptive in the front and opportunistic in the back, and has both the scheme and personnel — even without Micah Parsons — to challenge the Patriots' weak spots and personnel shortcomings along the offensive line and at the skill positions. | Edge: Packers

Patriots pass defense vs. Packers pass offense: New England's passing defense has been very good when playing man-to-man coverage (-0.36 EPA/dropback; 3rd), but suspect whenever Zak Kuhr opted to switch to zone (0.23 EPA/dropback; 30th). Finding the balance is a challenge, as he said himself last week, but it should be easier to do so against the Packers: Jordan Love is not a threat as a runner, which should play into the Patriots' hands. He also has three clear favorite targets in Christian Watson, Matthew Golden and Tucker Kraft, meaning that if New England can limit their damage and put pressure on an injury-plagued offensive line, they should be able to keep the NFL's passing yards leader in check. | Edge: Patriots

Follow every snap and discuss every decision with fellow fans on the SB Nation app.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Patriots rushing offense vs. Packers run defense: Taking both teams' production so far into account, this might be the Week 9 game with the least productive combined run games. Unsurprisingly, we are giving both defenses the edge. The first battle will see a New England offensive line that has had its issues blocking the run, particularly along the interior, go up against a generally stout run defense ranked in the top half of the league in yards per run (3.9) and EPA per run (-0.108). Rhamondre Stevenson has impressed so far as the clear RB1, but blocking consistency remains a concern. | Edge: Packers

Patriots run defense vs. Packers rushing offense: You think the Patriots run game has been bad? The Packers have been abysmal moving the ball on the ground. Obviously, it did not help that Josh Jacobs has been limited to two games following a domestic violence incident that remains under investigation, but the main issue — just like in New England — has been the blocking. The right side of the offensive line in particular has struggled, which is no surprise given that is dealing with some of the same personnel problems that have plagued the Patriots through most of the season. New England's run defense, meanwhile, has quietly developed into a solid unit ranking 14th in EPA per run (-0.104) and 10th in yards per attempt allowed (3.8). | Edge: Patriots

The Packers have been slightly better than the Patriots returning kickoffs and punts, and in kickoff coverage, while New England enjoys a minor edge covering punts. What tips the scale the home team's way in this one is the place kicking. Sure Andy Borregales has not set the world on fire in his second season as a pro, but his 88.2% combined success rate on field goals and extra points is still leaps and bounds better than Packers rookie Trey Smack's 77.2% — the worst such number among regular kickers in the NFL so far this year. Add that Borregales has familiarity with the Gillette Stadium wind patterns, and he looks like the more trustworthy option come Sunday. | Edge: Patriots

The Packers are an all-around solid teams that is doing the best with what it has available. The Patriots are in a similar boat, which is why both teams are 5-3 right now even though they have had to deal with some serious injuries over the first two months of the season. We are giving Mike Vrabel and company the smallest of edges, in part because their home record so far (3-0) is superior to Green Bay's on the road (2-2) — a sign of a team's abilities to adapt to travel and hostile environments. | Edge: Patriots

Despite being slight favorites, the Patriots beating the Packers on Sunday is not a given. If they come out like they did last week versus Miami, they might find themselves in a hole bigger than 10 points — and possibly too big to overcome. There is reason to be optimistic that that will not be the case again, but the message is clear: Green Bay is well-equipped to take advantage of any potential slip-ups, and New England needs to be on top of its game from start to finish in order to move to 6-3 on the season.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2632. NFL predictions, Week 9: Lucky 13 for NY Giants vs. Philadelphia?

The New York Giants have not beaten the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philly since 2013. That's 12 straight losses on the Eagles' home turf. Can the Giants end that streak this Sunday? Read on to see how the Big Blue View staff sees Giants-Eagles and the rest of the Week 9 slate unfolding.

I think I'll always be uneasy when the Giants go on the road to play the Eagles. Weird (and generally bad) things tend to happen to the Giants at the Linc. But dare I hope that some of the smoke from burning sage and the power of Danhausen lifting the curse on the Knicks leaked from Madison Square Garden over to the Giants' facilities this summer?

The Giants are favored over the Eagles on the road for the first time in recent memory, and John Harbaugh's record coming off of bye weeks is impressive. Cam Skattebo's hamstring is obviously a concern, and we have to respect the Eagles' playmakers and their ability to generate explosives. That said, I also have to believe Andrew Thomas, Jermaine Eluemunor, and Abdul Carter getting a much-needed break will have a positive impact on their play.

The Eagles were already struggling after the departures on their coaching staff, and fell into disarray with the retirement of Lane Johnson, the trade of Cam Jurgens, the loss of Jalen Hurts, and Saquon Barkley's injuries. Those excuses, however, fall flat considering the Giants are also without their starting quarterback, their offensive tackles have been gutting their way through injuries, their best pass rusher and a starting defensive lineman are on the injured reserve, and they've been dealing with injuries in their backfield and secondary — but have held it together and persevered.

I think I'll always have a (at least) a kernel of concern when the Giants play in Philly. But this seems like a great week for a statement game.

This is a must-win game for the Giants. Not because they can't win the NFC East if they don't – this division is bad enough to revive memories of the 2020 "NFC Least." It's because we don't know yet whether the Giants are frauds who've made a couple of plays late in games against bad teams, or a rising team that just has what it takes to win. The opening win over Dallas was impressive…but the Cowboys are a 3-5 disaster. The most recent win in Houston was impressive…but that team is now 2-5. In fact, the Giants haven't yet even played, much less beaten, a team that is currently above .500.

The Philadelphia Eagles are a train wreck this season, having lost many key players to retirement or injury and having parted ways with the best offensive line coach around, Jeff Stoutland. Still, that Eagles defense has Jalen Carter on the IDL, Zach Baun at linebacker, and quality defensive backs in Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean. Most importantly they have defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, whose two-high safety zone defenses with post-snap rotation have confused many quarterbacks and limited explosive pass plays.Will J.J. McCarthy be able to read that defense and exploit it, or is this the week he throws three picks and comes back to Earth?

The Eagles' offense hasn't really scared anyone this season. They traded A.J. Brown, DeVonta Smith and Jalen Hurts are out, Saquon Barkley is playing injured, and the formerly fearsome offensive line is a shell of its former self with future HOFers Jason Kelce and Lane Johnson retired and the rest of them injured or playing poorly. The wild card is that Joe Milton III will make his first start at QB for them. The Giants saw a little of him as a Cowboy in the final game last season, and Jalin Hyatt will have fond memories of a QB who actually completed a deep pass to him for a TD in college. Milton has a rocket arm and is more mobile than predecessor Tanner McKee, but the Giants should be able to limit him, if they can produce an effective pass rush. That said, Dallas Goedert always hurts the Giants, and Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, and rookie first-rounder Makai Lemon can make plays. At The Linc, you never know.

It's been 13 years since the Giants won in Philly. There's no excuse for them not to break that streak Sunday, and do so easily…unless they're frauds. I'll guess that they're not.

The New York Giants enter the matchup riding momentum after their bye week, while the Philadelphia Eagles are mired in a six-game losing streak and rapidly falling toward the top of the 2027 NFL Draft order. The Giants defense is playing well, and the offense received a spark in Week 7 against Houston.

Philadelphia's offensive line struggles to protect Tanner McKee, who isn't exactly fleet of foot. Philadelphia has averaged just over 14 points per game through this six-game losing streak. Philadelphia's defense surrendered 27 points to Washington, 38 to Dallas, and 25 to the Carolina Panthers over their last three contests. It's bleak in Philadelphia.

The Giants have not won in Philadelphia since 2013 — a 15-7 Giants' win where Josh Brown kicked five field goals, and Matt Barkley played for the Eagles. Eight of the Eagles' 12 victories were one-possession games, and New York had some brutal losses at Lincoln Financial Field. But new circumstances have arrived, and the Giants have an opportunity to end a disturbing chapter in this rivalry. Giants should comfortably win, 30-13.

The last time the Giants were favored at the Eagles was in 2009. The last time the Giants beat the Eagles in Philadelphia was in 2013.

That's a lot of history going against Big Blue as they travel to Philadelphia as 3-point favorites on Sunday.The Eagles are enduring a season from hell and after six straight losses, they sit at 2-6. They'll be starting their third QB of the season when Joe Milton gets the first start of his career on Sunday. Milton has appeared in five NFL games, and his last game action came against the Giants at MetLife Stadium in Week 18 last season, in mop-up duty of a meaningless contest with the Cowboys. He's a big guy with a big arm, and is a bit of an unknown quantity. For his career, he's thrown two touchdown passes and two interceptions. Philadelphia is obviously hoping he can spark an anemic offense that's mostly been without its star running back (who is quite familiar to New York fans), its top two receivers, and multiple first-string offensive linemen.

J.J. McCarthy draws his second start for Big Blue, who should be well-rested off the bye. Philadelphia's defense is still a capable unit, although it hasn't played all that well, in part because the offense can't sustain drives. If Philly has any chance to save its season, winning this game against the division leader is a must. I can see their defense giving maximum effort and posing problems for McCarthy, who I still don't trust completely.

This game scares me. The Giants are riding high after their big win over the Texans in Week 7 and Philadelphia is desperate. I also don't have confidence in Dominic Zvada if the game comes down to him, which it might. I'll give the G-Men the nod because they're the better team at the moment, but it won't be easy.

I was asked during a podcast appearance this week whether I was picking the Giants to win. I said yes, with great trepidation. This is Philly we're talking about, and whenever the Giants visit something always seems to go wrong.

This, though, is the first time in a long while where these teams have met with the Giants having a clear upper hand. The New York Giants being favored to win in Philly? Who saw that coming when the season started?

Good teams win games like this against struggling teams. I am going to trust that John Harbaugh and the Giants see the opportunity in front of them in the NFC East, and that they will take advantage Sunday of a team they should beat.

#2630. Ranking the World Series chances for last four MLB teams looking for first title after Brewers snap drought

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the fourth time in 10 years, Major League Baseball has a first-time champion. The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays in this year's Fall Classic to clinch the franchise's first title. They join the 2017 Houston Astros, 2019 Washington Nationals, and 2023 Texas Rangers as first-time champions across the last decade. That's a lot of new faces in the Fall Classic.

Milwaukee's title leaves four teams without a World Series championship, including those same Rays. One team was guaranteed to come out of this World Series with its first title and the Brewers won out. With the World Series complete, here is our authoritative ranking of the four ringless teams based on how close they are to winning their first-ever World Series.

2026 record: 58-104 (5th in NL West)2026 finish: Missed postseasonPennants: 2007

What do they have going for them? Coors Field is beautiful. I'll give them that. In all seriousness, the Rockies' new front office is run by competent baseball people in president of baseball operations Paul DePodesta and general manager Josh Byrnes. That's a pretty big step up from the friends-and-family crowd that ran the team previously. We saw some proof of concept too. A few pitchers on the staff, including Chase Dollander (who had UCL surgery in June), reshaped their arsenals this year in a way that suggests the Rockies are out of the Stone Age and getting caught up with modern analytics. We're starting to see signs the franchise is moving in the right direction.

What's holding them back? There just isn't enough talent throughout the organization. Dollander, Cole Carrigg, Hunter Goodman, Kyle Karros, and TJ Rumfield are the only 2026 Rockies who wouldn't be out of place on a World Series contender, and Goodman will go into the offseason as a trade candidate. The farm system is ranked middle of the pack and then there's the whole Coors Field situation. The team's home environment is a competitive disadvantage. How do you prevent runs and soft tissue injuries at altitude? Maybe Byrnes and DePodesta can figure that out. Coors Field is a real negative, though. The Rockies play half their games in a difficult and unique environment. Plus they're stuck in the NL West with the Dodgers.

When could they win their first World Series? The Rockies feel like they're two years away from being two years away, and even that might be generous. As promising as some of those signs were in 2026, the Rockies still have a long way to go to catch up to the most well-run teams, and an even longer way to go to amass enough talent to contend for a championship. It's reasonable to say no team in baseball is further from a World Series title than these Rockies.

2026 record: 91-71 (2nd in NL West)2026 finish: Lost NLDSPennants: 1984 and 1998

What do they have going for them? In Jackson Merrill and Fernando Tatis Jr., and wunderkind catcher Ethan Salas, the Padres have three excellent 20-somethings who are (or project to be, in Salas' case) above-average at their positions. Manny Machado is still a 30-homer guy and a premier defender at the hot corner even as he enters his mid-30s. There's Mason Miller too. San Diego has the game's best closer anchoring their bullpen. The front office has shown a knack for finding quality contributors on the cheap (Ty France, Gavin Sheets, etc.) and the new ownership group says it's ready to spend.

What's holding them back? The Padres have A LOT of money tied up in players on the back nine of their careers, including Machado, Xander Bogaerts, and Jake Cronenworth. Their best years are behind them and none of them are even halfway through their long-term contracts. The Padres are also very thin on the mound, particularly with Michael King (opt out) and Nick Pivetta (club option) not certain to return in 2027. GM A.J. Preller's aggressive wheeling and dealing has left the farm system very thin behind Salas. It's a top-heavy roster with a lot of downside risk in its most expensive players, and they're stuck playing in the same division as the Los Angeles Dodgers. The Padres won't get a Wild Card Series bye anytime soon.

When could they win their first World Series? It could be as soon as next season, though it will require a heavy investment from ownership in the pitching staff. Even retaining King and/or Pivetta will be costly, and the Padres need more behind them. With good health, good sequencing, and some savvy moves, sure, San Diego could win the World Series next season. That sure is a lot of ifs though, isn't it? There have been long stretches over the last few seasons when it felt like the Padres were a house of cards on the verge of collapse.

2026 record: 76-86 (3rd in AL West) 2026 finish: Missed postseason Pennants: None!

What do they have going for them? As disappointing as this past season was, the Mariners do have a lot going for them, namely their homegrown rotation (Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, Bryce Miller, Bryan Woo) and their homegrown up-the-middle (Colt Emerson, Cal Raleigh, Julio Rodríguez, Cole Young). If that's not a championship-caliber core, it's darn close to it. Dominic Canzone, Brendan Donovan, and Josh Naylor are a solid supporting cast, and if we exclude Anderson because he's made his MLB debut, the Mariners might have the best pitching prospect in baseball in Ryan Sloan. It also must be noted that the AL West is baseball's weakest division. An 87-win season might win you the AL West by 10 games in 2027.

What's holding them back? That homegrown core looks great on paper, but it did not perform as expected this past season, and a few of those players (Donovan and Gilbert, most notably) are only a season away from free agency. This team could look very different in a year's time. Also, ownership has held the line on payroll and kept the Mariners in the middle of the pack. Unless that unexpectedly changes, Seattle won't ever be in play for tippy-top free agents. The kind of free agents who can put a team on the cusp like these Mariners over the top. More than anything, though, it's the hard-to-explain underperformance from that homegrown core.

When could they win their first World Series? This was a very disappointing season, no doubt, but there is a reason the Mariners came into 2026 as the consensus best team in the American League. It's a talented roster loaded with prime-aged players, and the only significant free agent loss figures to be Randy Arozarena (that will be a big loss, of course). The AL West is so bad that it won't take much for the Mariners to get into the postseason next year. Get in and you can win.

2026 record: 98-68 (1st in AL East)2026 finish: Lost World SeriesPennants: 2008, 2020, and 2026

What do they have going for them? A very good team and a bona fide superstar in 23-year-old Junior Caminero, for starters. Jonathan Aranda, Liam Hicks, Victor Mesa Jr., and Chandler Simpson are strong building blocks on the position player side, and they have a tippy-top prospect in outfielder Theo Gillen. Grady Emerson, the No. 2 pick in the 2026 Draft, is also on the way. The Rays have a solid talent base in the big leagues, a rich farm system, the ability to pluck quality pitchers seemingly out of nowhere, and a new ballpark in Tampa proper on the horizon. There are positives aplenty here.

What's holding them back? Even with a new ownership group and the forthcoming ballpark, it seems unlikely the Rays will ever be a top spender. The best case might be a middle-of-the-pack payroll, and the less you spend, the less your margin of error. That's just the way it is. The Rays will never be able to plug holes or paper over mistakes with money the way other teams can. Also, they're stuck in a brutal division. Perhaps that eventually changes with expansion and realignment, but right now, the Rays have to contend with the Boston Red Sox, New York Yankees, and Toronto Blue Jays. That's a tough draw.

When could they win their first World Series? Next season. I mean, the Rays were in the World Series this year and they were the American League's best team almost wire-to-wire. They will need to replace free agent-to-be starters Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta; otherwise, the Rays will return every significant player next season, and the vast majority are on the right side of 30.

#2628. Former Good Good Golf executive sues company after being blamed for controversial ad

Good Good Golf's former vice president of brand and marketing, Jeffrey Lefkovits, is suing the company for $1 million after he claimed he was scapegoated for a controversial advertisement, according to The Athletic.

Lefkovits filed a defamation suit against the company and its former CEO and chairman, Matthew Kendrick, on Oct. 29. That suit claimed Lefkovits was wrongly blamed for the controversial ad that lost Good Good some key sponsorships. It also claimed that the violent scene in the advertisement was not "part of the original script Lefkovits approved," per court documents obtained by The Athletic.

The ad, which debuted in August, was meant to promote a co-branded driver from Good Good and Callaway. In it, Good Good Golf co-founder Garrett Clark runs over and shoves content creator Alexis Miestowski to the ground before sinisterly uttering, "Do not touch my new driver."

The ad immediately received criticism for promoting and making light of violence against women.

Good Good quickly pulled the ad, but it was too late. Callaway cut ties with the company and Good Good pulled out of a PGA sponsorship. Retailers also began pulling Good Good merchandise off store shelves due to backlash from the ad.

Lefkovits was eventually fired for approving the ad. In his lawsuit, Lefkovits claimed that the scene in which Clark ran over Miestowski was not in the original script when Lefkovits approved it. He then said he was out of the office when the ad was shot.

Lefkovits did approve the revised version of the ad, but claimed he did so after Callaway signed off on it. Amid the fallout of the ad, Callaway announced it would perform its own internal investigation into the company's approval process.

After having his employment terminated, Lefkovits said he was told his name would not be shared publicly. Shortly after he was fired, however, his name appeared in an article written by Front Office Sports.

That article tarnished Lefkovits' reputation in the industry and prevented him from finding new employment, per The Athletic.

"Every day that goes by without Defendants recanting their false statement, Lefkovits's ability to provide for his family is further diminished," the suit reads.

Good Good declined the comment on the lawsuit when reached by The Athletic. Kendrick, who stepped down as Good Good's CEO and chairman, did not respond to a message from The Athletic.

#2626. 'It was about each other': The Brewers and Pat Murphy admire the masterpiece they built

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Construction requires purpose.

Before materials are collected. Before architects render blueprints. Before the site gets chosen. There must be vision. The building of something, anything monumental, is less about machinery and labor. But about inspiration. It's the ultimate binding force. Human ingenuity powered by a bent for progress, a hope for excellence.

It's the purpose that fuels the willingness to build. And shared purpose produces the buy-in.

The work in progress that was the Brewers, a project eight years in the making dating back to Christian Yelich's arrival in 2018, was finally ready for the ultimate ribbon-cutting on Wednesday night at Tropicana Field. An unveiling of their finished work.

It took just five games to deconstruct the Rays. But it took eight years to build a team worthy of this moment.

And it took the Brewers 57 years to find the right construction workers to deliver the franchise's first-ever World Series championship.

"They decided to be uncommon," manager Pat Murphy told CBS Sports following his team's 4-1 Game 5 win. "And when they made that decision that it was about each other — when it's about each other and it's a team, you can accomplish anything."

Yelich, the 34-year-old captain, is at the center of all of this. He arrived in Milwaukee in 2018 and quickly became an MVP that season. A name that offered a glimmer of what the future could be. The Brewers made it to the NLCS that first year with Yelich, falling one game shy of a World Series trip.

Yelich was the ultimate building block for a club in dire need of one. He became the franchise. And the Brewers became perennial contenders, making the playoffs in every season with Yelich except 2022.

When the legs grew a little heavier with age. When the swing slowed. When the five tools became four, then three, then two. When the player who once carried a franchise had to learn what it meant to be carried by one.

His playing time dwindled. He didn't say a word.

Matchups against lefties began casting doubt over whether his name would appear on the lineup card. He didn't say a word.

And now, playing more of a supportive than a starring role, he's a World Series champion.

"It's an awesome feeling, man," he said, "and just so happy for our team, our city, all the guys, man. It's just it's the best feeling ever."

A man who has traveled a long road. You hear it in his voice. In his perspective. There's failure in it.

He spent a quarter-century as a college coach, most notably at Arizona State, where he was among the premier coaches in the sport. Much like Pat Casey at Oregon State, now also on the Brewers' staff, or Augie Garrido at Cal State Fullerton, Murphy was the kind of coach high school players dreamed of playing for.

But an NCAA investigation in 2009, one that ultimately cleared Murphy of unethical conduct but found fault with his oversight of the program, brought his college coaching career to an abrupt end.

And even after all of that, Murphy, drenched in champagne amid the lingering aroma of cigars, admitted something dumbfounding.

"I wasn't a very good coach," he said. "I had a lot of wins maybe."

Murphy joined the Padres as a special assistant. He managed the Eugene Emeralds, Tucson Padres and El Paso Chihuahuas. He even managed the Padres themselves on an interim basis before joining the Brewers in 2015 as bench coach under Craig Counsell, his former player at Notre Dame.

The teacher had to become a student again.

"There was so much I had to grow," he said.

There's David Hamilton, who returned to the organization that drafted him after a stint with the Red Sox. In Boston, he lost his way. His confidence disappeared. The game looked too fast for one of baseball's fastest players. The Red Sox tried to change him, encouraging him to pull the ball in the air, much as they do with many of their hitters. But it didn't work.

So when he returned to Milwaukee, Murphy had a message for him: Hit more ground balls to the opposite field. Bunt more.

"Really just trying to get on base," he said. "I think getting on base ultimately helps the team win."

There's Jake Bauers, a man who once considered retirement amid his struggles, now a World Series champion.

"It all changed for me when I realized it wasn't about me," he said.

There's Sal Frelick, the overlooked, undersized glue guy who, according to his manager, might have broken his hand after being hit by a pitch in Game 5. But Murphy trusted him to stay in the game.

"I said, when this last out is recorded and we're the last man standing, Sal Frelick will be on the field. That's just because of who he is," Murphy said.

Catcher William Contreras required a different kind of work.

Pet him, and he just might nip you, according to Murphy.

But that doesn't mean Murphy is afraid to put his paws on him.

He benched Contreras at the end of September for failing to hustle down the first-base line.

It was done with love. Murphy leads with love, but never at the expense of discipline. And with Contreras, he came to understand something else.

"The ones that are toughest to love need the love the most," Murphy said. "And he's a guy that needs the love, and it has to be real."

Contreras went on to put together one of the best postseasons in recent memory, becoming World Series MVP.

Champagne and beer filled the visitors' clubhouse. The cramped quarters were an afterthought amid the joy engulfing the room. The smell of victory permeated the air. The speakers boomed. The Game's "Hate It or Love It" blared over the sound system.

"Hate it or love it, the underdog's on top."

The Brewers, undoubtedly, were the underdogs. Despite winning 97 games the previous season, preseason projections pegged them for roughly 80 to 84 wins.

They traded Freddy Peralta to the Mets. Their rotation leaned heavily on young arms: Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Kyle Harrison, alongside an aging, oft-injured Brandon Woodruff.

They found a Cy Young Award winner in Misiorowski, the premium talent with a 105-mph fastball. Misiorowski tossed 5⅓ scoreless innings. Even without his typical swing-and-miss stuff, the right-hander limited the Rays to just two hits.

"This is crazy," a wide-eyed Misiorowski said on the field.

Because the Brewers have repeatedly found ways to survive the departures of players who once seemed indispensable. Josh Hader. Corbin Burnes. Devin Williams. Even manager Craig Counsell and former president of baseball operations David Stearns.

Yet Milwaukee, steered by Matt Arnold, who succeeded Stearns as president of baseball operations following the 2023 season, has continued to scout, draft and develop talent. Many of the anchors of this championship team were homegrown: Cooper Pratt, Jackson Chourio, Misiorowski, Brice Turang, Aaron Ashby, Abner Uribe, Garrett Mitchell, Frelick, Luis Lara and Henderson.

"We invest a lot of minutes in acquisition and development," Arnold said. "We've got to make sure that pipeline is very strong. That's our foundation."

Many have tried. Few have done it like Milwaukee.

Murphy stepped back onto the field early Thursday morning as a champion. The sea of Brewers fans that had overtaken Tropicana Field all week made their presence known. They chanted his name. They cried. Together. Because it had been a long time.

The cheers grew louder. The smiles wider. The cries more profound.

Murphy stopped. Soaking in his organization's creation. A vision realized. Something built, not bought.

"I needed them more than they needed me," he said of his players.

And yet, the Brewers aren't finished. A project eight years in the making still has work to do, much like the people who helped build it.

"We're always under construction," Murphy said.

#2625. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2623. Three reasons why the Brewers can repeat as World Series champions in 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers are the freshly crowned World Series champions for 2026. Add that trophy to a regular season body of work in which they won 103 games and achieved the best run differential in all of Major League Baseball, and it's clear the Brewers this season did all a team can do. The first title in franchise history will be remembered and cherished by the Brewers and their fans forever, and it was earned in every respect.

The celebrations won't soon end, and the post-Game 5 hangovers are still pulsing. Even so, it's time to turn our attention to the 2027 season and explore why the Brewers absolutely have the foundation necessary to do it all again next year. Here, then, are three reasons the Brewers can become repeat champions roughly one year from now.

Eyeball the Brewers' current contract obligations and service time tiers, and you'll find just six players are likely bound for free agency. Brandon Woodruff, Jake Bauers, JoJo Romero, and Gary Sánchez will be free agents soon. Elsewhere, Dustin May has a mutual option for 2027, which means he'll probably join them. Finally, Antonio Senzatela has a $14 million team option for 2027 on which the Brewers may pass.

Of those, the 31-year-old Bauers is the biggest needle-mover, as he's coming off a 2026 season in which he hit 26 home runs in 144 games and put up a WAR of 3.3. He does seem likely to move on, but the Brewers are more than resourceful enough to find comparable production from the non-premium position of first base.

Elsewhere, the Brewers should resist the temptation to trade away catcher, linchpin, and reigning World Series MVP William Contreras ahead of his walk year in 2027. The Brewers Way in recent years has been to part ways with core contributors around such a time, and that may be a temptation with Contreras, especially given Bo Naylor's presence on the roster. Contreras, though, is not easily replaceable given his skills behind the mask and his high level of production at the plate. An extension may not be something the Brewers will pursue – even though the ongoing CBA negotiations will probably lead to a new system that benefits teams like Milwaukee – but even if that's the case, they should keep their catcher and leader around for the final year of team control in the name of defending the belt and the title.

The champion Brewers, as a club that gets limited investment from ownership and is elite at player development, skews young even as they stand as the best team in baseball. Consider:

As for specific examples, they're not hard to find. Budding star Jackson Chourio will be in his age-23 campaign in 2027. Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will each be 25. Cooper Pratt, like Chourio, will be 23. The Brewers this past season got 16.4 WAR from those names, and Pratt and Henderson didn't even log full seasons.

Let's also note that Brice Turang, who led the Brewers this season with a WAR of 7.3, will be just 27 in '27 and thus should continue performing at a high level. This isn't just a matter of the Brewers being largely shielded from age-related decline next season. There's also the distinct possibility that so many of their 2026 pace-setters are still pre-prime and may have even better days ahead.

As though all of the above weren't enough, the Brewers right now have managed to thread this rare needle: they're the best team at the highest level and have one of the best collections of talent down on the farm. MLB.com in August ranked the Brewers as the third-best farm system in the game right now. FanGraphs ranked them third based on average prospect value. Baseball America at midseason likewise ranked the Milwaukee system third and after the season gave the system an "A" grade.

At an individual level, a number of premium Brewers prospects figure to arrive at some point next season. That list includes shortstop Jesús Made, who may be the top prospect in the game right now. Other 2027 arrivals may include talents like corner infielder Andrew Fischer, right-handers Tyson Hardin and Bishop Letson, and infielder/outfielder Jett Williams, among others. So many teams in contending mode have a fairly dry pipeline thanks to the low draft picks and the now-for-later trades that often accompany World Series aspirations, but that's very much not the case with lead executive Matt Arnold and the Brewers.

Celebrations of the work done in 2026 should be the focus right now for the Crew and their rooters, and once that dies down, they can all be further buoyed by the reality that the Brewers aren't going anywhere. The guess here is that the Brewers open the 2027 season – whatever it looks like — as the consensus favorites to do it all again.

#2621. Rory McIlroy assessed two-stroke penalty for improving lie, cards quadruple bogey in Abu Dhabi

Rory McIlroy had one blemish on his scorecard Thursday at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship. But it was an unsightly one.

McIlroy hit his second shot on the par-4 12th through the green and his ball rolled into a valley of rough. His third shot ran to the top of the slope, then traveled back down to this feet.

His ball nestled in rough, McIlroy placed his wedge behind the ball and — in the process — tamped down blades of grass. He went on to make what he thought was a '6' but turned out to be a quadruple-bogey 8 after being assessed a two-stroke penalty for improving his lie when he altered the grass.

"They showed me a video from 12. Hit my first chip shot from down on the bottom of the hill, then get up, came back down and rolled into a divot," McIlroy explained after officially posting a 2-under 70.

"And then as I went to sort of just get a feel for the lie, the close-up of the camera, you can see like a little piece of grass around the divot sort of lies down as I put my club down behind the ball, and it doesn't — I guess the grass doesn't return back to its original position.

"Obviously there's no intent. I play by the rules. I feel like this is never really — I try to do everything that I can to never end up in these positions. But just by looking at the video, like it doesn't look — it doesn't look very good. Obviously that wasn't my intent."

McIlroy added he was trying to get a feel for the lie.

"The ball is in a sort of bottom of a sandy divot," he said. "I'm trying to feel like if I can get a 54-degree, like, onto the back of the ball, but in the process, this piece of grass has sort of laid down, and it doesn't — you know, the technical — I guess the technical term for the rule is if you press down on the piece."

He contended that he didn't press down but told reporters he didn't want the perception to be that he "got away with something either."

"I'm happy to take a two-shot penalty and move on and move into tomorrow," he said.

Aside from the 12th, McIlroy had six birdies and no other dropped shots. His 70 put him eight shots off Francesco Laporta's lead and tied with playing competitor Eugenio Chacarra, whom McIlroy and Patrick Reed (74) are chasing in the Race to Dubai.

The Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship is underway at Yas Links in Abu Dhabi, UAE.

#2616. Lions, Vikings mic’d up video shows redemption arc for Jameson Williams

After a win, the Detroit Lions always release their own version of a "mic'd up" compilation from the game. Their "Sights and Sounds" videos are always worth your time, as they incorporate unique camera angles along with Dan Miller radio calls and mic'd up moments that you can't get anywhere else.

This week's episode detailing the Detroit Lions' 19-15 win over the Minnesota Vikings is can't-miss.

Obviously, it was an emotional game with Jack Campbell's traumatic injury, and I think One Pride Productions does a good job covering that moment with grace and compassion while properly conveying the gravity and emotions of the moment.

One other aspect of the game they uncovered was a moment of redemption that may have gone overlooked. This week, Lions receiver Jameson Williams was mic'd up, and it captured a couple of very interesting moments. Williams was involved in two extremely critical plays in the game. The first was his biggest mistake of the afternoon.

It was the fourth quarter, and the Lions led 12-7. They had just gotten an emotional fourth-down stop on defense, and it was up to the offense to extend their lead and bleed some of the remaining 13 minutes of game time. Facing a third-and-inches, Jared Goff ran a QB sneak up the middle for a first down. But Williams had not properly reported as off the line of scrimmage, causing the refs to call illegal formation. Detroit would not convert the third-and-6, and they punted it back to Minnesota.

As he was coming off the field, dejected, Williams was met with a coaching staff that had a message for him:

"You owe us," Lions coach Dan Campbell said.

"I know, I know, I know," Williams replied.

The Vikings capitalized on Williams' mistake, driving the length of the field to take the lead 15-12 with just under nine minutes remaining. That's when Lions receivers coach Scottie Montgomery repeated the message to Williams.

"You owe us," Montgomery said. "Go back, make a play. I know the frustration. It [redacted] sucks. But we know you're in. So stay in, okay?"

What ensued was one of the Lions' most impressive drives of the season. Detroit went 69 yards on just seven plays, led by five rushes for 57 yards—all of at least 9 yards. The cameras show Williams blocking is ass off the entire time. And on the first snap of Detroit's goal-line offense, Jared Goff pulled the rug out from underneath the Vikings defense with a play-action pass to a wide-open Williams.

As he sprinted toward the sideline following his game-winning catch, Williams reminded the staff of his redemption.

Campbell: "Way to pay us back! That's what I'm talking about!" Williams: "Hey! I owe you, don't I? I owe you, don't I?"

Williams: "Hey! I owe you, don't I? Montgomery: "Let's go!" Williams: "I still owe you! I still owe you! Aw, yeah! Aw, yeah!"

It's a great moment caught on tape by the One Pride Production crew. You can watch the entire video below:
