#2545. Midseason All-Rookie Team: QB Jalon Daniels leads team filled with multiple Browns, Jets

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The departure from a 16-game regular season eliminated a clean midway point to the NFL regular season, but there is a large enough sample size to assess the contributions of the rookie class through Week 8.

Reflecting upon the 2026 NFL Draft, there were 19 offensive and 13 defensive prospects taken in the first round. Although the No. 1 overall selection has yet to make his first start, several others are making a meaningful impact on their respective teams.

Daniels is the selection by default. He is the only rookie quarterback to appear in more than one game and the only quarterback with more than 36 dropbacks.

The undrafted free agent out of Kansas had some good moments. He looked crisp in three quarters against the Steelers, but accuracy waned in the game's most critical moments. His comfort is throwing to the boundary rather than attacking the middle of the field, but he would lock onto his first read, and defenders began breaking on it once they picked up on the tendency. When the sea parted before him, Daniels showed the foot speed to get chunks of yardage on the ground.

To be a viable quarterback long-term, Daniels must do a better job handling pressure. He was sacked nine times on 123 dropbacks because the protection was either not set to handle the blitz or he could not feel the pressure on his back.

He completed 60 of 98 pass attempts for 501 yards, three touchdowns, and five interceptions.

Preseason selection: Fernando Mendoza, Raiders

The running back position was more complicated than quarterback because each of the candidates has either missed time due to injury or is serving in a reserve role. Love leads all rookie running backs with 76 carries despite missing two games and is now actively dealing with an ankle injury that landed him on the injured reserve. His presence on the end-of-year All-Rookie team is very much in doubt.

Love shows good vision and does well breaking his feet down in space to leverage defenders. He is patient before making his move and has 11 receptions as well. Arizona's offensive line has left a lot to be desired. The Notre Dame product has been averaging 1.1 yards before contact this season, which is below average, according to TruMedia.

Las Vegas' Mike Washington Jr. has had some big runs on stretch plays to the boundary. San Francisco's Kaelon Black drew heavy consideration. Denver's Jonah Coleman has been a personal favorite, but the body of work is limited due to injury.

Preseason selection: Jeremiyah Love, Cardinals

Concepcion has the second-most receptions among rookie receivers but has nearly half of his receptions and 57.7% of his receiving yards over the past three games. It has taken some time to develop timing and chemistry with Deshaun Watson, who was errant on several passes in Concepcion's direction at the start of the season.

Among all rookie receivers, Concepcion ranks second in yards after the catch per reception (5.5), according to TruMedia. He is dynamic and elusive with the ball in his hands.

The Texas A&M product has 33 receptions for 352 yards.

KC Concepcion just has a different gear with the ball in his hands pic.twitter.com/bumtXpwWll

Preseason selection: K.C. Concepcion, Browns

Tate was the third choice, and the margins may be slimmer than one may expect of the leading rookie receiver. The No. 4 overall selection has four drops and three fumbles this season.

Tate has good size and the foot quickness to win out of the stem, but he generally has not been threatening downfield against man coverage. He was unavailable for Sunday's loss to the Bengals due to a shoulder injury; the first game of his career missed.

The Ohio State product leads all rookies in receptions (34) and receiving yards (413).

Preseason selection: Carnell Tate, Titans

Boston has slowed down a bit over the past month after his blistering start that led to some glamorous statistical and play-style comparisons. Most of his early season success was isolated to ball-winning downfield plays. In each of the first five games, he had a reception of at least 20 yards. In that metric, among rookies, he trails only his teammate, Concepcion, who has seven.

Boston is a classic X-receiver, but the Browns would be better served diversifying his usage as he becomes more comfortable transitioning to the NFL. The next step in Boston's growth is developing better chemistry with Watson and finishing plays. Boston has just one drop to his name, but there were a handful of others that could be classified as such. He is consistently open and a zone coverage merchant, but not always on the same page as his quarterback.

There are a variety of other pass catchers who deserve recognition, such as Omar Cooper Jr. (Jets), Germie Bernard (Steelers), Caleb Douglas (Dolphins), Antonio Williams (Commanders) and Malachi Fields (Giants).

Preseason selection: Denzel Boston, Browns

Sadiq has been a plus performer in both the pass and run games. He leads all rookie tight ends in receptions (17) and receiving yards (186). As a prospect, the ex-Oregon Duck was known for his play-making ability post-catch, and he has carried that trait into the league. Among all receivers and tight ends, Sadiq ranks second in yards after the catch per reception (6.0).

In the run game, he is a bulldog. He is constantly working and straining to sustain blocks and spring his teammates for bigger gains. At times, he could rein in that energy a bit better, but he has been a well-rounded asset for the AFC franchise.

In the preseason, Patriots tight end Eli Raridon was among those under consideration. He has been excellent for a rejuvenated New England team.

There have been a few rookies to moonlight as left tackles this season, but the possibilities boiled down to Kahlil Benson of the Chiefs, Jayden Williams of the Cardinals and Fano. Benson is a great story and incredibly valuable in the absence of former first-round pick Josh Simmons. However, Fano has a higher ceiling because of his athleticism.

Fano has a really natural feel for the game. He communicates and picks up exchanges well. He possesses the requisite foot quickness and ankle flexion to handle most of what is thrown at him. His issues are largely correctable, but his play strength still must improve.

Fano has been credited with two sacks and 18 pressures allowed on 311 pass-blocking snaps, according to TruMedia.

Preseason selection: Spencer Fano, Browns

Jacksonville's Emmanuel Pregnon and Proctor were candidates for different reasons. Pregnon has a better feel for the offense and consistently executes it well but does not possess Proctor's ceiling.

The former Alabama left tackle has allowed nine pressures and one sack in 186 pass-blocking snaps, according to TruMedia.

Preseason selection: Kadyn Proctor, Dolphins

A training camp injury to veteran Tyler Biadasz forced Slaughter into the starting lineup. Los Angeles' offensive woes can not be attributed to a single person, but the rookie has certainly been a flawed part of the line. TruMedia credits him with eight pressures and one sack allowed on 261 pass-blocking snaps, but more powerful interior players have given him fits with the bull rush. Slaughter has good foot mobility and can execute some of the blocks in space that have been asked of him.

Preseason selection: Jake Slaughter, Chargers

There was consideration to pencil in Ioane as the center given he spent some time there this season, which would allow Cleveland's Austin Barber to be the selection at right guard. Ioane and Barber have been the two best interior linemen this season. Baltimore intends to play the former at right guard, so he will align there in this exercise.

Although he is now dealing with an injury, TruMedia credits Ioane with seven pressures and one sack allowed on 210 pass-blocking snaps. Ioane plays with a sturdy base and looks for work when disengaged.

Preseason selection: Francis Mauigoa, Giants

Miller struggled in the preseason, which did not inspire much confidence. To his credit, he has responded and performed adequately for the Lions' offensive line. TruMedia credits him with one sack and 13 pressures allowed on 226 pass-blocking snaps.

Pittsburgh's run game has been a catalyst for the team's success, and Max Iheanachor's growth at right tackle is a contributing factor.

Preseason selection: Monroe Freeling, Panthers

Halton has been impactful in the run and pass games. He has three run stuffs, which is the second-most among rookie interior defenders. He has also turned eight pressures into two sacks. San Francisco drafted two defensive tackles last season, but it has been Halton giving the NFC franchise a jolt.

Preseason selection: Kayden McDonald, Texans

Gill-Howard is not contributing much in the run game, but his 15 pressures and two sacks lead all rookie interior defenders. He got the final nod over the Jets' Darrell Jackson Jr.. Gill-Howard's value is exceeding his sixth-round selection for a franchise fighting to keep pace in the NFC North.

Preseason selection: Christen Miller, Saints

Bailey leads all rookies with 5.5 sacks and 26 pressures. The first-year player out of Texas Tech has a spin move that he likes to use, but diversifying that rush plan will be the next stage of growth. He shows an ability to set the edge in the run game and has some violence in his hands but occasionally loses gap discipline. His 15.4% pressure rate is best among rookies, according to TruMedia.

Jacas has been a ball of energy for the Patriots. He has shown an ability to win with a variety of moves but will also play down the line to finish plays on the backside. Jacas has good speed and power and can break down blocks. He has been a personal favorite at the position thus far.

According to TruMedia, Jacas has a 15.0% pressure rate, which is second-best among rookies with at least 100 pass rushing snaps, according to TruMedia. He also ranks second in pressures (23) and sacks (3.0).

Preseason selection: Reuben Bain Jr., Buccaneers

The options at linebacker are plentiful. Reese plays square to the line of scrimmage and is able to slip blocks to fit run gaps. He has some shock in his hands and does well setting up pass rush moves when his number is called.

The injury to quarterback Jaxson Dart could have effectively ended New York's season, but players like Reese have stepped up. He is a well-rounded prospect with elite athleticism. The Giants could honestly utilize him more as a pass rusher, but there is no need given the presence of Kayvon Thibodeaux, Abdul Carter and Brian Burns.

Preseason selection: Arvell Reese, Giants

Styles looks like he stepped out of central casting for an NFL linebacker. He is a fluid athlete who is able to build speed quickly and trail in coverage. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones hails from the Brian Flores coaching tree, so Styles has been a part of the rush plan. He has just 45 pass rush snaps, but has converted eight of those into pressure.

He has 54 tackles, one sack, one forced fumble and one interception ths year.

Preseason selection: Sonny Styles, Commanders

One benefit to being the writer of a story is the creative liberties that come with it. In the preseason, a third cornerback spot was incorporated to get Caleb Downs on the field, but the linebacker group has been the most impressive, so this team will incorporate three.

Admittedly, I was not the biggest fan of Daniels as a prospect. He looked a bit stiff to fulfill a safety role but also did not look like a natural fit at linebacker. The Oklahoma product does a good job slipping blocks to fit run gaps and rush the passer. He has the range to play sideline to sideline. Daniels has 53 tackles, one sack, one fumble recovery and one interception.

Tampa Bay's Josiah Trotter, Miami's Jacob Rodriguez, Tennessee's Anthony Hill Jr. and Daniels' teammate, Harold Perkins Jr., have also represented the position well.

Preseason selection: Caleb Downs, Cowboys

Delane was one of the easiest selections for the team. He is aggressive playing downhill in run support, but also has elite awareness of his surroundings. The No. 6 overall selection builds speed quickly to stay in-phase and is physical at the line of scrimmage. Delane is at his best playing the ball on arrival.

It was a long day at the office against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but that is true of most any cornerback. Eighty-nine of his 227 receiving yards allowed were against the Seahawks, according to TruMedia.

Preseason selection: Mansoor Delane, Chiefs

There have been multiple cornerbacks who have expressed potential this season: Hezekiah Masses (Raiders), Brandon Cisse (Packers), Davison Igbinosun (Bills), Will Lee III (Panthers) and Muhammad. Muhammad had been present in first-round mock drafts in the past, but faltered in his final season with the Longhorns.

Injuries in the Bears secondary led to Muhammad being called into action, but he has made the most of his opportunity. Muhammad must do a better job finishing tackle attempts. He has a 19.2% missed tackle rate, according to TruMedia.

Preseason selection: Brandon Cisse, Packers

Cleveland has slowly expanded upon McNeil-Warren's role. He has lined up over the slot at times and, at other times, has been the single-high safety. His breakout game was on "Thursday Night Football" against the Steelers, but ironically, Pittsburgh humbled him a bit in Week 8. McNeil-Warren has great range and has shown that in his ability to close on the football.

The former MAC star should have recorded his first career interception and returned it for a touchdown against the Ravens, but he was busy planning his celebration before securing the catch.

Preseason selection: Dillon Thieneman, Bears

Wheatley has been reliable for the Panthers defense. There are few wasted steps in coverage, and he is rarely out of position. The safety can do a better job wrapping up tackles but plays square to the line of scrimmage. Carolina has been riddled with injuries, particularly in the secondary. The presence of veterans Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn would make life a lot easier for the rookie.

Wheatley has one interception and one forced fumble to his name.

Pittsburgh's Robert Spears-Jennings has outperformed his seventh-round selection. He should earn more playing time over the second half of the season. Chicago's Dillon Thieneman is also worth acknowledgment.

Preseason selection: Treydan Stukes, Raiders

#2543. Brandon Aiyuk files to be reinstated, will report to 49ers facility this week, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk is taking the steps necessary to return to the field. This week, ESPN reported he had hired agent Drew Rosenhaus to represent him, and now, he has reportedly turned in paperwork filing to be reinstated. Adam Schefter says Aiyuk will report to the 49ers' facilities on Friday.

"Brandon is healthy and ready to get back on the field," Rosenhaus said.

If Aiyuk is reinstated, the 49ers could trade or release him. General manager John Lynch said 10 months ago it was safe to say the wide receiver had played his last snap for the 49ers. The franchise would like to pick up some compensation in parting ways with their two-year-old headache, but it remains to be seen if any team would offer anything for him. ESPN reported that if Aiyuk is reinstated, the most likely outcome is the franchise releasing him.

This strange saga began when Aiyuk tore his ACL in October 2024. He was placed on the PUP list prior to the 2025 season as he continued to rehab, but 13 months after his injury, it was reported that the 49ers had voided the $27 million of 2026 salary guarantees in his contract. Aiyuk apparently had not been checking in with the team, sticking to his rehab schedule or doing what his contract required of him. Aiyuk was placed on the reserve/left squad list in December.

Aiyuk spent this past offseason taking shots at the 49ers on social media, and acting as if he were going to reunite with his college quarterback in Jayden Daniels and sign with the Washington Commanders. However, the 49ers still owned his rights, so Aiyuk had to file for reinstatement and then be acquired via trade if his Washington dream were to come true. Aiyuk refused to complete these steps in the offseason, but now, he's playing ball.

Aiyuk established himself as one of the best wide receivers in the NFL in 2023, as he caught 75 passes for 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns on the way to Super Bowl LVIII. His 3.1 yards per route run that year ranked No. 3 behind Tyreek Hill and Nico Collins, and his 81.3% of receptions going for a first down or a touchdown ranked first in the NFL.

The offseason following the Super Bowl appearance, Aiyuk orchestrated a "hold-in" during training camp, which eventually led to the four-year, $120 million extension he was after. That 2024 season, Aiyuk reached 50 yards receiving in just one of the seven games he played in before tearing his ACL.

#2542. Five things we learned from Victor Wembanyama's '60 Minutes' interview, including why he loves going barefoot

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It is increasingly rare in the NBA (and professional sports as a whole) for a star athlete to sit down for an extended, on-the-record interview. While athletes have found other means of communicating with fans, such interviews can offer rare, less-filtered glimpses into what the player is going through both on and off the court.

Few players in any sport can say they've had a more eventful last few years than Victor Wembanyama. The San Antonio Spurs star reached his first NBA Finals last season and, in the process became a villain to fans across the world rooting for the New York Knicks to end their 53-year championship drought. He ultimately fell short in that matchup, but is now ascending to his seemingly inevitable place as the future face of the NBA. With the 2026-27 season only just beginning, Wembanyama sat down with CBS News' "60 Minutes" to discuss his career thus far. Here are five highlights:

Sponsorships are a standard component of the superstar experience. Wembanyama has been intentionally choosy about who and what he has aligned himself with. In the past, he has made it clear that he would never work with a soda company, for instance, because he does not want to promote unhealthy products. In Sunday's interview, he took aim at athletes promoting different vices.

"I think as an NBA player, and if you're amongst the stars of this league, you really make your career whatever you want to make it," he said. "Of course, you're always going to do your best on the court, the best that you can. But on the side, you can choose to be the influencer, you can choose to be the philanthropist, you can choose to be the guy who's gonna promote gambling and alcohol. You can choose whatever you want."

When asked what choice he has made, Wembanyama reiterated that health is his guiding principle. "I think my choice isn't final because I'm still growing as a person," he said. "But I want to promote healthy things, and by healthy, I don't just mean the food, but healthy habits, things that make people's lives better. And in the future, things that also make society better."

The public perception of Wembanyama changed quite a bit over the course of a single postseason. He was one of the league's breakout stars last season, and his consistent success over the widely disliked Oklahoma City Thunder earned him quite a bit of admiration from casual fans. However, his hard fouls, first in the second round against the Minnesota Timberwolves, and then later, of course, against the Knicks, turned him into a villain overnight. While Wembanyama claimed he wasn't paying attention to that noise during the Finals, he did learn from it after the fact.

"It showed my limits more than anything else," Wembanyama said. "Going out there, you need to play basketball, you don't need to beat the shit out of people. If you want to win at least." Had the Finals lasted beyond five games, he might have learned the lesson in more convincing fashion.

In Game 5, Wembanyama committed a foul on Jalen Brunson that many argued was flagrant after the fact, but because the Knicks ended the series then and there, the NBA was not forced to review it. Wembanyama was just one flagrant foul point away from a suspension for a hypothetical Game 6 at Madison Square Garden. Now, Wembanyama wants to make sure he doesn't put himself in that situation again.

Shoes are perhaps the single most important piece of equipment in a basketball player's arsenal, yet whenever possible, Wembanyama prefers not to wear them. "I try to walk barefoot as much as I can, and wear minimalistic shoes," he explained. For him, it's a matter of health.

"Because big men have always had feet problems," Wembanyama said, alluding to the NBA's lengthy history of injury-prone centers. "I also find more and more that feet are responsible for so much more that goes on. It's funny because I was just talking to a rookie. I went to practice barefoot and he sees me walk in without shoes and he goes, 'I did not know you could just not wear shoes.'"

Wembanyama believes that "if you've got good foot strength, which brings a good foot posture, everything else can level up the right way. Knee, hip, back and everything." Thus far, his methods seem to be working. His longest absence in the NBA came as the result of a blood clot in his shoulder, and while he has dealt with some of the same lower body injuries that many players are enduring in the pace-and-space era, he managed to maintain awards eligibility in both his first and third seasons. He has not yet missed a game this year.

Wembanyama has lived in the United States for more than three years now, yet he acknowledges how atypical his American existence has been. "When they ask me what it's like to live in the U.S., my answer is always, well, I don't know. I don't live a normal life in the U.S.," he said. "I live the life of an athlete, a rich person, the life of somebody that's gonna have everything taken care of no matter what I do, really. It's not the life of a regular American. It's the best country to be an athlete in."

That atypical experience has given him a unique perspective on life in the United States, and he sees both pros and cons compared to what he grew up with in France. "Good is how it feels like you're never judged for being ambitious," he argued. "Bad, I would say, I think the social interactions are more shallow here. Not as in-depth as they are in other countries."

Wembanyama is hardly the first foreign-born star to thrive in the NBA, but he's on pace to outshine all those who came before him. The NBA has obviously had plenty of international MVPs and champions, but it has never had a foreign face. Eventually, Wembanyama is expected to stand alone atop the sport, once the old guard of legends like LeBron James and Stephen Curry retire. That puts him in a somewhat unique position to attempt to influence the way stars conduct themselves moving forward. He is already seemingly attempting to do that in the way he chooses sponsors, and only time will tell how much more of his perspective will trickle down to his NBA contemporaries.

Wembanyama has never been shy about how excited he was to land with the Spurs. He called it "a winner's franchise," and cited both the team's history with French players and the presence of "the greatest coach of all time" as draws even before San Antonio won the 2023 NBA Draft Lottery. While that coach, Gregg Popovich, has since retired after suffering a stroke, Wembanyama got to start his career with Popovich on the sideline, and he explained that his greatest lesson was "about humility."

"He often said something when we were in film: after a win, you're rarely as good as you thought you were. And after a loss, you're rarely as bad as you thought you were," Wembanyama said.

That is a lesson that will have to persist this season, as the Spurs attempt to pick up the pieces following their Finals loss to New York. San Antonio blew double-digit leads in all four of its losses in that series, and the film will inevitably showcase many of the ways in which they were deficient against the Knicks. But the Spurs got to the Finals in the first place, well ahead of schedule, and while they should internalize what didn't work, they should hold onto what did.

It certainly seems as though they've done that this season, winning four straight after losing their first two games of the season. The Spurs are currently the championship favorite following a rash of injuries to the Thunder, and maintaining an even keel across the season will be essential in ensuring that they maintain that favored status.

#2541. Browns' Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol: Shedeur Sanders potentially in line to start Week 9 at Saints

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson entered the NFL's concussion protocol Tuesday morning, the Browns announced. Watson, who passed concussion evaluation after taking a helmet-to-helmet hit during Sunday's loss to the Steelers, told team doctors he started feeling concussion-like symptoms Monday night.

Deshaun Watson has been placed in concussion protocol pic.twitter.com/ViiyRHMct8

Should Watson be unable to play in Week 9 against the Saints, the Browns would likely turn to second-year pro Shedeur Sanders.

Watson briefly left Sunday's contest in Pittsburgh after a spotter called down to the sideline for Watson to be checked out after Jaquan Brisker's helmet-to-helmet hit (which was flagged). Sanders entered the game briefly before Watson returned. Watson finished the 27-6 loss with 324 passing yards but also eight sacks and zero touchdowns.

Brisker flagged for hit on Watson #Steelers #NFL pic.twitter.com/FCOv8QtjJA

The Browns say they also evaluated Watson for a concussion after the game and again Monday morning, per league rules. However, when Watson reported his symptoms to the team on Tuesday morning, Cleveland immediately put him in the protocol.

Sanders, 24, could start Sunday in a crucial game for the Browns, who are 5-3 this season. He has appeared in two games this year, but only for five snaps. He has completed all three of his passes for 2 yards.

Sanders did get considerable playing time as part of Cleveland's quarterback carousel last year, appearing in eight games (seven starts). He threw seven touchdown passes and 10 interceptions while completing 56.6% of his passes. He had some impressive performances, including a three-touchdown day against the Titans, but struggled overall. Out of 36 quarterbacks with at least 200 pass attempts, he was last in completion percentage, touchdown-to-interception rate and passer rating.

Sanders lost the quarterback battle to Watson this offseason, but should he be called upon to start, he'd be in a much better offensive ecosystem than he was in last year. The Browns have upgraded their offensive line and wide receivers, with rookies Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion impressing. The Saints could potentially provide a soft landing spot, too: New Orleans' defense ranks 28th in both yards per play and yards per game.

#2540. Organized Chaos: Bournemouth’s Possession Principles Against Nottingham – MH

von Next Generation am 28.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League,Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

On Matchday 23, the two surprise teams of the Premier League faced off. Nottingham, unbeaten in their last nine matches, has impressed this season with outstanding defensive work. Bournemouth, coached by Andoni Iraola and now unbeaten in 12 games, takes a completely different tactical approach compared to most other teams. In an interview with TNT Sports, Guardiola remarked: “Today, modern football is the way Bournemouth, Newcastle, Brighton, and Liverpool play.” What exactly are these teams doing differently? Bournemouth’s approach will be analyzed in detail based on this match.

Bournemouth’s coach, Andoni Iraola, is a former player under Marcelo Bielsa at Athletic Bilbao. Bielsa, widely known in the Premier League as the coach who led Leeds United to promotion, gained recognition for his style of play characterized by exceptionally high intensity in all phases of the game. According to Iraola, his own footballing philosophy has been significantly shaped by his former coach Bielsa.

In an interview with Sky, back when he was still managing Rayo Vallecano, Iraola stated: “I was very lucky to play for him (Bielsa) for two seasons as a player. I think he has another vision of football. They were two very good seasons for us, and, for me, it was a different knowledge.” He also explained: “I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him. I use a lot of things, especially with the ball. Offensively, his teams are very dynamic. He is willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder, offensively.”

Iraola’s tactical concept can be described as “organized chaos.” The aim is not to implement a positional system with perfect patterns of play. Instead, the focus is on creating problems for opposing teams by generating chaos. The idea is to force the opponent into unfamiliar, uncontrolled phases of play. A particularly important concept within this is highly intense, man-oriented, hybrid attacking pressing, designed to force the opponent into quick turnovers and a fast-paced, direct game.

„It is true that we like, and we perform better, in high-tempo games. We need to run a lot. We don’t need so much control, not in every single play, but I think we have the legs, we have the willingness, to go up and down.“ – Iraola

Accordingly, Iraola’s style of play could face challenges against deep-lying teams that deliberately thrive on minimal possession. These teams don’t need to engage with Bournemouth’s high-intensity game but can instead remain compact out of possession. They are not required to build up play from the back under Bournemouth’s pressing to maintain controlled possession but can focus on their own offensive transitions. This season, Nottingham has been one of the most successful teams in executing such an approach. Consequently, it was particularly intriguing to observe how Iraola’s Bournemouth would operate in possession against Nottingham’s deep block.

Iraola describes his philosophy in possession as follows:

“We have to prepare [positional] patterns, but we cannot just prioritise them. If you can see that you don’t have a teammate ahead, forget about the pattern, just drive the ball and try to force things to happen. I want him to attack first.”

Here lies the challenge I encountered while analyzing the game against Nottingham: how do you describe intentionally provoked chaos, where there are barely any fixed patterns? Only a few predefined sequences can be identified within the positional framework. The crucial question, therefore, is: what reference points structure Bournemouth’s possession play, and which principles of play create this chaos? Or, put simply: what “tools” does Iraola use in his style of play? To answer this, the positional framework of the game against Nottingham will first be examined.

Starting from a nominal 4-2-3-1 formation, Nottingham defended out of possession in a 4-4-1-1 or 4-5-1 structure. Nottingham focused primarily on defending and largely conceded possession to Bournemouth, a characteristic approach for the team. Under coach Simoes Espirito Santo, Nottingham has averaged just 40% possession this season.

Bournemouth, meanwhile, operated in possession with a positional 2-4-4 or 2-3-2-3 structure, featuring wide wingers and full-backs. From this setup, Bournemouth attempted to break through Nottingham’s deep block. On the (left) No. 10 position, Kluivert stood out with his exceptional dribbling ability and high agility. Central midfielder Christie alternated between the deeper right half-space as a right-sided No. 10 and the No. 6 position.

Nottingham was often forced back into their own half from an initially higher defensive pressing. When Nottingham attempted to press higher, Bournemouth’s center-backs positioned themselves wide, and goalkeeper Kepa moved up to form part of the back line. This made it nearly impossible for Nottingham’s lone striker to put significant pressure on the ball carrier. As a result, Nottingham dropped deep, retreated, and refrained from pressing the ball-carrying center-backs.

„I sometimes value much more a player carrying the ball and forcing things to happen. I think when you play too positional – one, two touches to find a free man – you sometimes lose the initiative from the players to just take their man on and attack the spaces.” – Iraola

This approach meant that Bournemouth’s center-backs were frequently required to dribble forward against stationary opponents, forcing defenders to commit. This often created 5v4 or 4v4 situations on the flanks, caused by the strong lateral movements of striker Ouattara and attacking midfielder Kluivert, combined with the forward dribbling of the center-backs. When no passingoptions were available, the team didn’t rebuild play, as is typical for positionally oriented teams. Instead, Bournemouth’s left center-back, Huijsen, was occasionally seen dribbling directly at the opponent’s last defensive line. It can be concluded that one of Iraola’s key principles of play is to attack vertically with the ball as early as possible.

Center-back Huijsen dribbles toward the final defensive line himself due to a lack of better-positioned deeper passing options.

The situations on the flanks during the center-back’s dribbling were played out in various ways. Sometimes the ball was passed to the wide player on the wing, who was tasked with taking on a 1v1 duel. This player was consistently supported by the full-back in a dual-width setup.

Particularly noteworthy were the positional rotations of the 3-4 players on the flanks. Full-backs, attacking midfielder Kluivert, striker Ouattara, and the winger frequently rotated out of their positions, occupying different spaces. What stood out was the consistent presence of a dynamic deep run within these rotations, forcing the opponent to cover the run and thereby creating space between their players.

The positional rotations with deep runs create passing options.

For example, the left-back Kerkez, during the center-back’s dribble, occasionally made deep runs into the half-space. Similarly, attacking midfielder Kluivert was often involved, sometimes shifting laterally to receive the ball and then driving forward at pace to attack the defensive block.

Nottingham responded to this from the 30th minute by attempting to apply more pressure on Bournemouth’s ball-carrying center-backs. The 4-4-1-1 shape was adjusted by removing the man-marking on defensive midfielder Adams. Instead, Nottingham transitioned into a 4-4-2 setup, aiming to position Adams in the cover shadow and step out earlier to press the center-backs. However, Bournemouth’s goalkeeper Kepa played so high in the back line that he was still able to connect with the now even wider-positioned center-backs, allowing them to continue dribbling forward.

The goalkeeper stepping into the back line creates a 4v2 situation, allowing the center-backs to dribble forward with less pressure from opponents.

“I would say they have the freedom to risk a little bit in the dribbles.“ – Iraola

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s possession game is diagonal, vertical dribbling. These serve as a chaos factor and are constantly utilized across all positions. As long as no teammate is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal, players are given the freedom to dribble. The skillful dribblers on the wings, the striker, and attacking midfielder Kluivert fit perfectly into this principle. The spaces opened up through the aforementioned rotations, particularly between the opposing players on the flanks, were mostly attacked through dribbling rather than passing.

The core idea behind this focus on dribbling is closely aligned with the concept of relationism. The goal is to make the team’s decisions less predictable for the opponent and to create a certain degree of chaos. Traditional positional play often limits players’ individual freedom, which reduces the element of surprise. However, Iraola’s execution of possession football differs significantly from relationism.

Instead of using a tighter structure to encourage combinations between players, rotations and larger distances between players are used to create spaces intended to be attacked through dribbling. It is crucial that these dribbles are always executed as vertical actions, continually putting the opponent under defensive pressure and thereby opening up other options.

Due to the larger spaces on the flanks, many dribbles are initiated on the wing, supported by the dual-width occupation of the winger and full-back. To enforce a successful follow-up action against deep-lying opponents, proper box occupation is a fundamental requirement. Iraola’s teams often flood the opponent’s penalty area with up to seven players, forcing the opposition right in front of their own goal. The goal is not necessarily to find the open player but to increase the likelihood of winning the ball after a cross in the penalty area. Second balls also play a significant role in this approach.

Risky dribbles have the additional advantage of provoking more frequent transition moments. When the opponent tries to transition offensively, they lose their compact defensive shape. Bournemouth’s flexible rest defense allows the ball to be immediately recovered after a loss of possession. Bournemouth’s rest defense typically consists of 3-4 players, depending on the attacking structure. In addition to the two center-backs, defensive midfielder Adams and the inverted, far-side full-back provide cover. If both full-backs or Adams are involved in the attack, Christie drops deeper to provide support and shifts closer to the ball.

On one hand, it’s important to highlight the excellent sense of positioning from the two central midfielders, Adams and Christie, in anticipating potential turnovers. Their ability to read these moments and their spatial awareness lead to many successful counter-pressing actions. On the other hand, the immediate pressure applied to the ball-carrying opponent after a turnover is notable, leaving the opposition with little opportunity to create controlled possession phases.

As a result, Nottingham’s offensive presence in the first half was minimal. Successful offensive transitions by Simoes Espirito Santo’s team were extremely rare.

The rest-defense structure in the 21st minute consists of the inverted Kerkez, the shifting defensive midfielder Adams, and the center-backs. At the same time, the ball-near teammates position themselves in response to the dribble in a way that allows them to immediately apply pressure if needed.

Another key principle of Bournemouth’s play is that after regaining possession, the first action is immediately directed forward. In contrast to traditionally positional teams, control is not sought through possession in chaotic situations but rather through constant transitions. The goal is to prevent the opponent from regaining their structure and settling into their usual rhythm. This creates intense pressure for Bournemouth’s opponents. As a result, Bournemouth often didn’t even need to break down Nottingham’s defensive block because the opponent never had the chance to regain their typical structure.

After recovering the ball, Bournemouth consistently looked to play forward into pressure. When positioned deeper (closer to their own goal), players in the forward zones immediately made runs into space to create vertical passing options. Even if the Bournemouth player who regained the ball was immediately under pressure, the first action was directed forward.

If necessary, a long ball was played toward the opponent’s defensive line, with a focus on winning second balls. This pressing game with an emphasis on second balls—often referred to as “kick and rush”—generated additional forced transition situations, preventing the opponent from finding their usual shape. The fact that four of Bournemouth’s five goals against the typically deep-lying Nottingham team came from deliberately provoked transition moments highlights the effectiveness of this approach.

In the second half, Nottingham switched to an attacking press in an attempt to create more scoring opportunities and overturn the 1-0 deficit. However, Nottingham was unable to pin Bournemouth in their own half as planned. Instead, Bournemouth played targeted long balls to one of their four advanced attackers or to the half-high positioned full-backs. Through a combination of winning second balls, dribbles, and central midfielders following up for lay-offs, Bournemouth was able to quickly progress into space and control the game from their own half. This led to Bournemouth scoring their second and third goals in quick succession. The final result was a resounding 5-0 victory for Iraola’s side.

So, what exactly causes the chaos in Bournemouth’s possession play? In summary, it is a combination of the principles discussed: playing vertically as early as possible; dribbling diagonally and vertically as long as no player is better positioned toward the opponent’s goal; and making the first action after regaining possession a forward one. The focus on vertical zones (reference point: opponent players) and second balls (reference point: the opponent’s goal) creates an intense and dynamic style of play that prevents the opponent from settling into their usual structure. Bournemouth is further aided by their attacking press, which was not analyzed in detail in this article but consistently provokes additional transition situations.

What can other teams take away from Bournemouth’s possession approach without abandoning their own philosophy? One lesson is the courage to consistently seek depth, provided the team has appropriate counter-pressing structures in place. Additionally, the dynamism of individual actions at Bournemouth is remarkable. Rarely have I seen such explosive runs into depth from other teams.

The final question is: what do the teams mentioned by Guardiola in the aforementioned interview have in common? All of them attack the depth quickly and frequently, making the game incredibly dynamic and intense. This forces the opponent to make decisions faster. After all, the main difference between good and very good players is the time it takes to make a good decision.

My recommendation is to watch games from 30 years ago. It quickly becomes apparent that football has become faster and more demanding.

“For me, the players are better than in 2003. They have to do the same things, but much faster. The physical demands are ridiculous. I doubt I could have played at this rhythm.” – Iraola

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2538. Three notable decisions from NBA's rookie-scale extension deadline: Thunder seemingly give up on lottery pick

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Normally, the NBA's deadline for teams to pick up team options on their rookie-scale contracts is Halloween. As the end of October came on a weekend this year, however, it was pushed to Monday. This deadline is usually relatively uneventful. Former first-round picks living up to expectations, or with obvious paths to improvement in the near future, have their third- and fourth-year options picked up. Obvious busts tend not to.

Of course, teams inevitably get these decisions wrong from time to time, and that sends promising players to unrestricted free agency at the end of the season in question. The most notable recent example came in 2021, when the Phoenix Suns declined their third-year option on Jalen Smith, whom they'd selected at No. 10 overall ahead of players like Devin Vassell and Tyrese Haliburton less than a year earlier. Smith has since grown into one of the NBA's better shooting big men for the Chicago Bulls.

I bring this up because a handful of notable team options were declined ahead of Monday's deadline, setting some interesting prospects up for unrestricted free agency next summer. The NBA is more financially cautious than it has ever been thanks to the aprons, forcing teams to make hard decisions on young players before their futures are fully written. There will inevitably be more Jalen Smiths in the years to come, and a few declined options from the past few days stand out as candidates.

There's a degree of validation that comes with being drafted by the Oklahoma City Thunder. Sam Presti thought Nikola Topić was worth the No. 12 overall pick in 2024, and while Presti is hardly infallible, he's the NBA's best general manager by a wide margin and his instincts are usually worth imitation. Oklahoma City didn't decline Topić's 2027-28 option because he's played poorly. They declined it because he's barely played at all.

He missed his rookie season with a torn ACL. He missed most of his second getting treated for testicular cancer, only appearing briefly in 10 games. He has not yet played this season because of back surgery. It is entirely possible that Topić simply never stays healthy enough to reach his potential as a player. It is also entirely possible, especially on a Thunder team that suddenly needs minutes wherever they can find them, that he starts living up to that potential the moment he returns to floor.

Oklahoma City's injuries represent the greatest opportunity of Topić's career. The team that drafted him averaged 66 wins in his first two seasons. There weren't going to be many minutes available for him anyway. Now, if he can just make it back onto the court, he should get real on-ball reps for the team with the best player-development track record in basketball. He can set himself up for a real opportunity in unrestricted free agency next summer.

The Thunder were never going to be able to afford him long-term considering all of their other obligations, so in that sense, they've arguably done Topić a favor. If they'd picked up his option and then cap dumped him later, he might have wound up in a bad basketball situation. Now, he has the rest of the season to show what he can do and the freedom to shop his services to the teams that need them most.

Guard minutes were readily available for the Utah Jazz over the last two seasons. Isaiah Collier took plenty of them, averaging over 25 minutes per game in each of his first two seasons. Even with Darryn Peterson in the fold this year and Ace Bailey taking on a bigger role next to Keyonte George, Collier has still been featured pretty heavily by backup standards. Case in point: through six games, he is averaging the most minutes on the roster (18.5) of anyone who has not yet started a game.

Yet the Jazz surprisingly decided to decline his option for the 2027-28 campaign on Monday. What this means for the Jazz next season still isn't clear. Utah still has plenty of room below next season's projected luxury tax, but that space could evaporate quickly if they elect to re-sign restricted free agent Brice Sensabaugh and/or use a mid-level exception. Perhaps the Jazz want to seek out a veteran backup. They may also prefer to minimize their investment in ball-handlers to ensure that both George and Peterson play on the ball when the other rests. The Jazz have plenty of shot-creation in the front court. They can afford to be stingy at backup point guard.

Collier arrived in the NBA as a high-level playmaker. His scoring and defense just haven't kept up. But he was once the No. 1 recruit in his high school class, and there's plenty of tape on him already for other teams to study. The talent is here even if the role potentially wouldn't have been in Utah.

Tidjane Salaün was the highest draft 2024 Draft pick (No. 6 overall) to have his fourth-year option declined, but that probably works in favor of a potential reunion between him and the Charlotte Hornets over the summer if both sides want to pursue one. When a player has a rookie-scale option declined, his original team can still re-sign him in free agency ... but only up to the salary he would have made on that option. Salaün's fourth-year salary would have been $10.4 million or so.

That's a much heftier figure than later picks, and it creates a bit of a win-win scenario for the Hornets. If Salaün doesn't live up to that figure, they aren't forced to pay it to him and could try to keep him at a lower rate. If he does, however, then they are at least getting a productive player at a scarce position for this season. If nothing else, that's a valuable trade chip at the deadline.

Salaün's overall minutes have gone down in each of his NBA seasons thus far, but he's playing better than he ever has in that smaller role this year. That's not saying all that much, but his combination of physical traits, theoretical ball-handling and shooting and willingness to play hard at least offer the outline of a useful, all-around wing. This is a player archetype that teams are usually eager to take chances on. Whether it's with Charlotte or somebody else, Salaün will probably get another chance.

#2537. Jadeveon Clowney mock trades: Cowboys reunion headlines four deals Texans can make before NFL trade deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the NFL trade deadline less than a week away, the hot stove is officially boiling. More and more names are being bandied about with each passing day. Some of them are big and some are smaller, but it seems like things could get pretty wild ahead of Nov. 10.

One name that has been floated in recent days is Houston Texans edge rusher Jadeveon Clowney. ESPN reported earlier this week that the former No. 1 overall pick's name has surfaced in trade discussions.

The Texans are sitting at 2-3, three full games back of the Jacksonville Jaguars in the AFC South and 2.5 games back of the final wild card spot. Clowney himself has played sparingly, appearing on only 37% of Houston's defensive snaps so far this season. He's also been fairly unproductive, recording just 1.5 sacks, two tackles for loss and four quarterback hits.

His pressure rate of 13.0%, though, indicates he's been a bit more effective than his counting stats, as he ranks 58th out of 262 players who have rushed the passer at least 50 times so far this season, according to Tru Media. The sample is very small, as Clowney has just 69 pass-rush snaps.

Still, given Clowney's age (33 years old) and relative lack of production, it's hard to see him generating much in the way of a trade return for the Texans. It's most likely that he would net a late-round pick at most, and perhaps only a swap of picks. The Texans sent one of their 2027 seventh-round picks to Cleveland in 2025 and another to Detroit this past offseason in the David Montgomery deal, but have one incoming from the Chargers, so that is the pick we have them sending out in each deal.

As for a few teams that could make sense for Clowney, here's a list.

The Niners have already given their defensive line a boost by trading for DeForest Buckner, and they should welcome Nick Bosa back into the fold soon, if not this week coming off their bye. But they're still just 21st in the NFL in pressure rate, according to Tru Media, and they have been dealing with injuries along the defensive front all season. Adding another capable rotational player off the edge could give them an extra boost ahead of a potential playoff run.

The Chiefs have bigger needs, with the most obvious one being wide receiver, but that doesn't mean they can't use at least some help in the pass rush department. George Karlaftis has 34 pressures this season, but R Mason Thomas, Felix Anudike-Uzomah and Ashton Gillotte have combined for only 42, according to Pro Football Focus. Adding another body to the mix could have some merit. The Chiefs have a 2027 sixth-round pick incoming from the 49ers, likely very late in the round, which they can send out here.

To be clear, the Cowboys should almost certainly not be buyers ahead of the deadline. They are 3-5 and going nowhere fast. But we know that Jerry Jones doesn't operate that way. He fears irrelevance more than anything else, and the Cowboys are in danger of becoming irrelevant this season. Clowney was in Dallas last year and racked up 8.5 sacks but the team elected not to re-sign him because of scheme fit concerns, but with the pass rush mostly not getting home, perhaps the Cowboys would bring him back. Dallas sends out a 2028 pick here because the 2027 sixth-rounder is headed to Pittsburgh in the Joey Porter Jr. trade.

The Giants are in first place in the NFC East and apparently going hunting for all kinds of players at the deadline. With Brian Burns out for the year, the Giants check in 31st in pressure rate, per Tru Media, and they could use some help for Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux coming off the edge. If they allocate more resources to other positions, it could make sense to go for a cheaper option on the defensive front. The Giants have an incoming sixth-round pick in the 2027 draft from the Jacksonville Jaguars, and that's likely to land pretty late in the round.

#2536. Robinson Canó Jr., son of eight-time MLB All-Star, agrees to $1 million deal with Marlins, per reports

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Marlins have reached a preliminary agreement with 16-year-old Robinson Canó Jr. that stands to make him part of the club's 2028 international signing class. The agreement is worth $1 million, reports Mike Rodriguez.

MLB rules state that an international amateur free agent player is eligible to sign with an MLB organization between Jan. 15 and Dec. 15 of his signing class year. He must turn 17 before Sept. 1 of the year in which he signs.

Canó Jr., a highly regarded shortstop out of the Dominican Republic who bats right-handed, is the son of former MLB great Robinson Canó. The elder Canó spent parts of 17 seasons in the majors, the majority of which came with the New York Yankees. Over that span, Canó earned eight All-Star selections and three Gold Gloves; racked up 2,639 hits and 335 home runs; and won a World Series ring as a member of the 2009 Yankees. He went on to sign a large free-agent contract with the Seattle Mariners, where he played from 2014-18.

Canó's career total of 68.7 WAR would under normal circumstances make him a strong candidate for election to the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, two suspensions for positive PED tests make it unlikely he'll get a plaque, at least while he's on the BBWAA ballot. He last appeared in the majors in 2022 as a member of the Atlanta Braves.

Canó Jr. is also the grandson of José Canó, who appeared in the majors with the 1989 Houston Astros, which puts him in line to be a third-generation major leaguer.

#2535. Draymond Green gets first ejection of season after sparking Warriors-Suns scuffle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Draymond Green made it to November (barely) before earning his first ejection of the 2026-27 NBA season.

On Monday night, Green took exception to getting knocked over by Phoenix Suns center Khaman Maluach posting up in transition and got up and tackled Maluach, wrapping him up with both arms and throwing him to the ground -- Maluach still made a basket for an and-1. Dillon Brooks then ran over to confront Green, which unsurprisingly led to a brief scuffle between the two and Green was eventually given two technical fouls and ejected in an eventual Warriors win.

Draymond Green was assessed a double technical on this play and was ejected. pic.twitter.com/uCmsTQxmcX

"I was just trying to de-escalate it," Brooks said. "He was just tweaking all game."

The ejection is Green's 31st of his career and he now has three technical fouls this season, tied for the most in the league. Once a player reaches 16 technicals in a season, it triggers an automatic one-game suspension.

Without Green, the Warriors surged back from a double-digit second-half deficit to get a 116-113 win thanks to Stephen Curry's heroics with 34 points and a huge game off the bench from Charles Bassey, who scored 19 points and pulled down eight rebounds in 22 minutes due to Green's absence.

Bassey's 19 points in 22 minutes off the bench on Monday night equals Green's 19 points in 159 minutes of play this season. Green does lead the Warriors in assists (6.3 per game), and the offense hums around him with Curry and rookie star Yaxel Lendeborg combining for more than 50 points per game.

With the win, Golden State improved to 5-3 on the season and now sits in seventh in the Western Conference standings early in the season as the Warriors try to claw their way back to the playoffs for the first time in three seasons.

#2534. Ravens trade candidates: Three quarterbacks Baltimore should consider amid injury crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Baltimore Ravens sit in a dangerous position, as they lost their top two quarterbacks to injury, and their third option is also questionable. On his first passing attempt in the eventual 36-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills, Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury that required surgery, landed him on injured reserve and could end his season. Then, Tyler Huntley suffered a season-ending turf toe injury as well.

That forced undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano into the lineup, who completed 10 of 21 passes for 91 yards and one interception vs. Buffalo. However, he's nursing an ankle injury and is considered questionable for the Ravens' Week 9 matchup vs. the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday. That led Baltimore to add Kedon Slovis and Austin Reed to its roster.

While Fagnano will likely join Anthony Brown as the only undrafted rookie quarterbacks to start a game for the Ravens, should the team consider chasing a legitimate starter prior to next Tuesday's trade deadline? While Baltimore does reside in last place in the division with a 4-4 record, the season isn't over yet. Let's examine three quarterback options for the Ravens to consider.

The Arizona Cardinals demoted Jacoby Brissett from starter to third-stringer this week, as Mike LaFleur is moving forward with Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck as his new No. 2. Brissett was benched for Minshew in the third quarter of the Cardinals' Week 8 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys, who sparked the offense with three touchdown passes in the fourth quarter to get the game to overtime. The Cardinals won that game in the extra period, leading LaFleur to make the decision he did.

Brissett has not been terrible this season. He's completed 63.3% of his passes for 1,719 yards, 10 touchdowns and seven interceptions in eight games. His 75.6 yards per game to Trey McBride entering Week 8 were the most by a QB-TE combo since 1970 (min. 15 games). Brissett isn't going to be raking in Pro Bowl votes, but he's a borderline starter in this league that would be an upgrade over an undrafted rookie or career third-stringer.

This would be the most intriguing swing of the bat for general manager Eric DeCosta, as Anthony Richardson is the option that offers the most upside. The former No. 4 overall pick out of Florida hasn't made a start since 2024, but he's one of the most athletic quarterback prospects we've ever seen. Obviously, it hasn't gone according to plan for him with the Indianapolis Colts. The 24-year-old quarterback is 8-7 as a starter, having completed 50.9% of his passes with 11 touchdowns and 13 interceptions in 18 total games played. Availability and consistency have been major issues for Richardson, but a change of scenery could do wonders for him.

Before you write Richardson off as a complete bust, consider the impact J.J. McCarthy is having early on for the New York Giants. Why couldn't Richardson thrive after his long-awaited trade? Plus, Richardson is a dual-threat athlete who could pair well with Derrick Henry. He averaged 40 rushing yards per game in his first two seasons, and scored 10 touchdowns on the ground as well. Give me the read option every play.

Tyson Bagent of the Chicago Bears has been floated as a trade candidate for the Ravens given his familiarity with new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. Bagent has truly been one of the most fascinating stories we've seen in the NFL over the past couple of seasons. Undrafted in 2023 out of Shepherd University -- a Division II school in Shepherdstown, West Virginia, Bagent did enough with Chicago in his first preseason to earn a spot on the final 53-man roster. As a rookie, he was called upon to make four starts, and even defeated No. 1 overall pick Bryce Young and the Carolina Panthers in prime time.

Bagent signed a two-year, $10 million extension in 2025, but has struggled this season. He threw for 268 yards and one interception in the Week 4, 23-12 win against the New York Jets, then threw for just 87 yards and two interceptions in the 31-7 blowout loss suffered at the hands of the Green Bay Packers the following week. Bagent's struggles look even worse considering that 38-year-old Case Keenum threw for 247 yards and two touchdowns in a primetime upset of the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 3. If Caleb Williams had to miss another start at some point, you have to wonder who Ben Johnson would start at quarterback this time around.

One question to consider is what would the Bears want for Bagent? If Ryan Poles wants a fourth-round pick for him,it should be "thanks but no thanks."

#2533. Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren

Inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

Inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

The primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be quickly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

Even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

This three-man buildup creates new passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

Due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

One of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

While striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

The pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

Once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

Especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2532. Tarik Skubal contract predictions: Ace's new deal could break multiple MLB records for a pitcher

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tarik Skubal is about to become a very, very rich man. The two-time Cy Young winner and arguably the best pitcher in baseball hits free agency this winter, and it stands to reason that he'll break the record for highest-paid pitcher in MLB history, both by total value and average annual value.

By total value, Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds that record thanks to the 12-year, $325 million contract he signed ahead of the 2024 season (we're eliminating Shohei Ohtani from the running for obvious reasons, though his 10-year, $700 million deal would clearly lead the list).

As for AAV, Ohtani again tops the class at $70 million a year, but for those who only pitch, Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander share the record at $43.33 million annually.

The expectation is that Skubal will break both records, even as the owners try to tamp down on spending in the ongoing CBA negotiations. Just how high could those figures go? CBS Sports experts pulled out their calculators.

Mike Axisa: Seven years and $325.5 million. That's $46.5 million per season and it would break the records for average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million) and total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) for a pitcher. I would expect there to be an opt out because those are just the cost of doing business these days. Maybe even multiple opt outs. Scott Boras loves to break records, though, and this contract allows him to break two.

Dayn Perry: I'll say eight years, $350 million. Likewise, that sets the record for total contract value and AAV for a pitcher. Normally, I'd ding him a bit for those elbow problems in his walk year, but he was mostly dominant after returning ahead of schedule. I also think Skubal will benefit from an aggressive pre-lockout market and from a pretty thin free agent class overall.

Matt Snyder: Eight years, $400 million. This gets him the record deal for pitchers both in terms of the guarantee and the average annual value. I'm probably going too low on the years, but I feel like teams have been burned so many times before on the length of pitcher deals due to injury that this holds down the market a bit. Ever so slightly. I do think there will be opt outs after years three and five.

#2531. Robert Kraft named one of five contributor nominees for 2027 Pro Football Hall of Fame class

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Patriots owner Robert Kraft is one of five contributor nominees for the 2027 Pro Football Hall of Fame class, it was announced Wednesday. The Contributor Subcommittee whittled the field down from 42 options to five, and it will meet again on Nov. 17 to decide on one of the five remaining nominees to advance to the full Selection Committee. The Selection Committee will then announce its selections for the 2027 class shortly before the Super Bowl.

Kraft is joined by Ralph Hay, Virginia McCaskey, Doug Williams and John Wooten.

Kraft received the subcommittee's vote last year to advance to the Selection Committee vote, but he was controversially left out of the 2026 Hall of Fame class. Kraft has been eligible for the Hall of Fame for years, but last year was the first time he had advanced out of the subcommittee. Former Patriots coach Bill Belichick, in his first year on the ballot, did not get selected for the Hall of Fame, either.

Kraft, 85, has owned the Patriots since 1994. Under his ownership, New England has won six Super Bowls and appeared in five more, including last season's loss to the Seahawks. Prior to Kraft's ownership, the Patriots had only been to one Super Bowl, which it lost. In addition, Kraft has been a key member of several NFL committees, and he helped lead the creation of Gillette Stadium, which opened in 2002.

In 2024, ESPN detailed Kraft's long struggle for a spot in Canton, with various voters pointing to Spygate (when the Patriots taped the Jets' practices), Deflategate and dismissed charges after Kraft's two visits to a Jupiter, Florida, massage parlor as reasons why Kraft hasn't been inducted.
